This is Mr. & Mrs. Zutty Singleton, Tape 1. We have got to start again because that's all distorted, you know. So I think Zutty if you would begin at the beginning and say where you were born.
Well I was born in Bunkie, Louisiana.
Bunkie?
Yes, that's right.
BUNKY?
KIE.
KIE.
That's right. On 14th May 1998. You want to play that back?
No, let's do a little more.
Alright. You know I can't even
think.
Well, now your parents, were they musicians in any way?
Well my Aunt Carrie.
She more or less brought you up didn't she?
Yes, she's the one that partly raised me in a way because she was an old school teacher and I used to go to Bunkie and (Upper Lousay?) and Mamou (Marmout?), that's in Louisiana.
Let's see what we've got now. Now your Aunt, she played the piano?
Yes she did.
Did she encourage you in music?
Well she sure did because my mother did also you know. Because my aunt bought me my first set of drums. Yes.
When did you first sort of begin to feel that you wanted to play the drums?
Oh, from way back. I was a real small boy.
What, you used to beat on chairs and things?
Yes. I used to beat on chairs
and things like that. And used to get the chair rounds out of the kitchen chairs and make sticks and play, you know. Beat them out.
And I suppose seeing bands marching in the streets, did that have something to do with it?
Oh yes indeed. Sure, I used to love to follow those bands you know. They called it the second line you know.
What sort of bands would they have in Bunkie, sort of marching bands?
No, not in Bunkie. This was in New Orleans. Yes, yes.
Well when did you go there?
Oh, when I was about ten years old.
Oh, ten.
Went there to live, to stay, yes.
And your cousin was a big influence on you.
What is that?
Your cousin, I say he was a big influence on you.
Yes, he was. Well I used to call him my uncle. You know like we told you before,
because when you taught school, you see, my mother and my Aunt Carrie and my Uncle Willie, they were supposed to be brothers and sisters, you know.
But who was Willie actually, your cousin?
He really was my cousin, yes. But during that time if you were married you couldn't teach school, you know. And so that's why Willie became my uncle, you see?
He was your Aunt Carrie's son, was he?
That's right.
I see. How much older than you was he?
Oh, he was about 7 or 8 years older than I.
That was a lot.
Yes.
When you're a kid.
Why sure.
And what was his second name?
Bontemps.
Oh yes.
BON....
TEMPS?
TEMPS, that's right, yes. And he used to take me to different rehearsals, you know.
What did he play?
He played bass and guitar. And banjo.
This was after you'd gone to St. Louis, to New Orleans?
To New Orleans, yes. He played with the old original Jack Carey's band for a long time.
Was that a jazz band or a marching band?
Yes, that was a jazz band.
It was?
Of course they had a big marching band also. Most all the band, you know, they used their name (men?) you know, Jack Carey.
Was Jack Carey any relation of Mutt Carey?
That was his brother.
Oh! What instrument did he play?
Mutt Carey?
No, Jack Carey.
Jack Carey played trombone. Because they used to call 'Tiger Rag', instead of calling it 'Tiger Rag', they used to call it, 'play Jack Carey.' Because he was famous for his 'Tiger Rag' you know.
Well, this is before Nick La Rocca and people would put their name on Tiger Rag?
Yes I imagine so.
Well what do you, how old would you be now?
Well at that time I must have been about 14 or 15.
Well that brings us to about 1913 and that's before the original Dixie Land Jazz Band had ever been heard of.
Well, I don't know. They were, the Dixie Land Band was around during those times. I can't go on any further.
That is one thing that I like, That let's you know if you left the, if you've left the volume up on the ......... When did Monroe come in the picture?
Well (Viney Monroe?) looked like she used to work for my mother in Bunkie.
Oh yes.

See then from then on she just raised me right on up. You know, Viney Monroe, because she had two sons and a daughter and they didn't call her by the real name. It was Sissy Viney, Bud Viney and Daniel Viney. They'd call....
By her first name?
Yes.
Yes?
Yes. But her name was Viney Monroe.
Was she a musician in any way?
No.
Oh, but she just, she helped bring you up?
Helped bring me up. Take me around you know. Yes, she worked with me, believe me.
Well now, had your father, when you went to New Orleans had your father left your mother?
Yes, he had.
He had? He'd taken off?
Yes.
How well did you ever know him?

Well I knew him pretty good. Because I remember he used to go hunting a lot of times, you know. He'd bring rabbits in and everything. That's why my mother didn't like rabbit. Because she was cleaning the rabbit and he moved, he jumped, you know. Because my father had been hunting you see, and she couldn't stand a rabbit after that because the rabbit wasn't quite dead, you know. Just startled her a little.
Well it's funny though, you know people here, you talk about eating rabbit pie or anything, they, they think it's a joke. And I always used to like rabbit.
Yes. I did too. I loved rabbit. I sure did boy because I remember when we were playing with Big Eye Louis in New Orleans. And they were great cooks, all of the guys in the band, and huntsmen.
Which band was this?
What?
Which band was this?
This was Big Eye Louis.
Oh, Big Eye Louis's band.

We were playing at Palms Road House and each night some guy would bring something that he had cooked or something like that. And the way old Big Eye Louis could fry rabbit. Boy, and he'd have the garlic all through it, you know. Oh, it was delicious.
And Maurice Decou Durante, he was a great huntsman also. And Walter Decou who was the piano player.
I suppose you could really walk out, I mean it wouldn't be far out of New Orleans before you could go hunting?
That's right.
In those days.
In those days. You see all of that country is built up now.
Yes, yes. Well when you went to New Orleans, now who had really taught you drums by the time you get your first professional job?
Oh well, I'll have to say Steve Lewis.
Yes, I see. Yes.
Yes, Steve Lewis. He encouraged me a lot. We played the drums, because we used to play little house parties and things like that.
What did Steve play again?
Piano.
Piano.
He played with A.J. Piron (Roth?).
Oh yes.
Who made 'Sister Kate' famous.
Oh yes.
'Purple Rose of Cairo.' And old Steve couldn't read, boy, and he played with all those good musicians.
Really?
He used to play at (TRANCHINA'S?)
out at Spanish Fork.
He'd got a good ear then.
Yes, he must have had an ear.
Naturally Piron (Roth?) had the violin and give him those little (parts?) and things like that. Of course everybody in that band was a good musician. Like Pete Bocage (Roche?).
Pete (Roche?) was the clarinet player?
No, the trumpet player.
Trumpet?
Yes.
Oh, oh.
Played the trumpet. And Tio, Tio was with that band.
Well was that the father or the son?
Well that was, well Tio had an uncle that played in the French opera.
Oh!
You see, Papa Tio they used to call him. Tio was just a big fine clarinetist.
Well he was the one that taught all the people wasn't he? Like Jimmy Noon and all those?
Yes, yes.
Didn't he teach all of them?
Yes. They all loved Tio. That's where the 'Mood Indigo' came from, Tio.
Did it?

Yes. You see, because I met Tio's daughter out in a country town here in New York State, and she was still kind of salty with Barney Bigard because he let Duke have this thing of, he let Duke have this thing, 'Mood Indigo' because they claim, Barney told me that Duke put more, a little more something to the tune.
Yes.
Said Duke added a little more .....
Yes, I'm sure. But the main body of the theme and everything was, yes. Well that's the sort of thing that's happened over and over again.
I saw .....
Cheers.
Cheers and love.
Love.
Love the most. Just recently I was going, on somebody's recording they had Barney's name with Duke Ellington as the composer.
Oh 'Mood Indigo?
Yes. Then I looked at another one and it didn't have Barney's name on it, it just had Duke Ellington.
Well Barney's name is on it officially, yes.
Yes, because on one of those albums we had there is somebody's name.
They made like it was just given away. Tio gave it to Barney.
But didn't Mills have his name on it too?
Who?
Mills.
Maybe so.
I thought that was Ellington, Bigard and Mills?
Maybe so.
Well on those albums we have somebody playing 'Mood Indigo' and they have Barney and Duke Ellington.
It just look like Tio just gave it away.
And when we came across another one it only had Ellington's name on it. So, Ellington and Mills, or something like that.
It puzzles me a little bit, Zutty. This at the Rose Bud guy has you your first professional job theater?
The Rose Bud theater.
Oh, well now you were talking about the Lyric Theater, is that somewhere else?
No, that's downtown. That is downtown.
Well, where was the Rose Bud?
The Rose Bud was up in my neighborhood. It was just a movie house.
Oh, I see.
See, so Steve Lewis and I got the job in the Roseland playing for the movies, you know.
The Rose Bud.
The Rose bud. Yes. And oh we stayed there quite a while.
Did you tell the story about how you hired Louis? To work for you in your band? In New Orleans?
Well we haven't got to that yet.
I think we told that because...
No, I don't think you told it on the first mishap. I don't remember you telling me that. But after the Rose bud then, what did you, you had to accompany the pictures?
Yes.
Well that was good playing wasn't it?
Yes. It was good, very good training. Timing and.....
But of course, you had to do a lot of Effects as well as straight drumming I take it you had to do all those noises, didn't you?
Sure. We had to imitate you know the picture. A big crash would come or something like that, I'd try to follow it, you know. Zully
I think that's why they had all those different equipment that the other drummers had never seen or heard of. Like the ratchet and all that.
Well what did you do, whistles and things?
All kind of whistles.
(He uses ?) his whistle.
Steam boat whistle. I'd blow that steam boat whistle, you know. Try to come out a little even there you know.
Well did you have chains to rattle?
Chimes?
S: Uh uh.

Chains. Chains. I remember, often remember seeing a picture called The Covered Wagon, you know. That was when they first started to get into the sound affects in a big way. And they would have sort of like when they cracked the whip, you know. And then they had the chains, their horses moved off, they had chains rattling. But of course, you were all set to imitate horses hooves.
Those bells now, what did you use them for? I've got them over there in the case, those bells that you had?
Well that was for a Christmas show in Connie's Inn. You see I bought that when I was in Connie's Inn.
You still use them. He uses them during the holidays.

For Christmas, Santa, Hal Bacquet (Falcon) was Santa Claus I believe. Big guy, he sure didn't look like Santa Claus. And every now and then Hal would have me come in with the sleigh bells. (SOUND OF BELLS IN BACKGROUND). Well, I bought them in 1929.

Well you know something, you're just about in the fashion now because that's all they're doing. If you went to see Herbie Wein's Hancock's band at the George (Wingate) festival. Now these people play saxophones and flutes and everything. But half the time they are standing up just jingling bells. You know, it's really getting kind of funny. There is nothing going on except people jingling and playing percussion.
Now just like when I was on the boat with Fate [MARABLE] We had a tune we used to play 'Stop Thief' and I'd have to make shots like, you see. They
were shells you know, empty shells. But I had to hit on these things. Some kind of introduction we'd have this 'Stop Thief' you see. And I'd have to shoot these the pistols off you know.
Oh, you'd fire them in a pistol?
Yes.
It would be a blank?
Yes, a blank. Blanks, yes. But they were all on a aboard like see, and I could hit them you know.
Oh?
Yes. All on a aboard.
What would you hit it with then?
With a mallet.
Oh? And they'd go off like a pistol shot?
They'd go off like a pistol shot.
Very exciting. (LAUGHTER).
And like that slap stick?
Yes?
Well, we got Ted Weems' record on that 'Sobbing Hearted Blues'.
Right.
And see, I used to have to hit that slap stick, you know, in the spot, you know.
Well what was the slap stick used for really? What was the chief purpose of that?
Slap stick was used for everything in vaudeville. Everything like, just like a slap, you know, you hit it.
Oh, I see. The comedians smack and you would have to ....
Yes, we would have to.......
That's funny, I never realised that.
Well Zutty has in his bag of tricks, I'm telling you.
Yes, well you.....
I had a lot of things.
Oh, the ( ?) drum was never used.
Chinese gong. You see, and I used to use that right in the theater. And when I started playing in big bands well I still used it.
Yes, yes. That's really where that whole sort of tradition came from then? Out of the theater? Really, didn't it?
the kldron
Yes, and I had to slack some horn for an automobile. Oh, I just had so much stuff you know.

Well what I really meant by that was that when you get those first sort of jazz bands with those funny noises and things they used to do, that's really coming out of the theater isn't it, that's what I mean.
Sure, that's right out of the theater. I even had a duck call.
Yes.
Yes.

Because that, I mean that didn't belong in say the dances in New Orleans where they had string bands and everything in the early days for the whatever you know, the Quadrills etc, there wouldn't have been any of that.
There wouldn't have been, that's right. You had to be in the theater to dig that. You see, because different comics wanted different effects.
Also I would think that they, accompanying the movies had a lot to do with it.
Why sure. Sure.

Now Ethel Walters she tells, brought she's told it several times that she xrxkxxxxxuxgxkxx out of Zutty New Orleans. She liked him so much at the Lyric Theater. She didn't bring Zutty out of New Orleans.
But she taught me the Charleston.
But she said she's the one that ......
Where did she teach you to the Charleston?
In the theater. In the theater.
Yes, he was so great that she brought him out of it of New Orleans.
Well was this when you moved downtown to the Lyric?
That's where he was playing.
Well how long after you were in the Rose bud did you go down to the Lyric?
Oh, gee, a long time.
Oh, a long time?
Yes a long time. Because I was just playing with different little groups, you know.
Different little bands and things. You see, because I didn't go to the Lyric Theater until I left the Cadillac Cabaret.
Where, you see it says worked occasionally with John Robichaux. Where would that have been?
That was at the Lyric Theater.
Oh that was at the Lyric?
Yes, that was at the Lyric.
But all this was before you went in the Navy?
No.
No.
No?
When he came out of the Navy. He was in the Navy when he was seventeen years old.
Well now, we haven't got that, why did you decide to go into the Navy?
Because I admired the sailors. And they looked so clean all the time. And I just said, this is for me. I'm going to join the Navy.
His mother had to sign.
It was more that than the matter that you wanted to see the world then?
Well sure, he wanted to see the world too.
And adventure, he loves adventure and travel. I mean from a kid......
A travelling man. (LAUGHTER).
(unintelligible) the hard way.
Yes, but you see he's not a kid that wanted to go in the Navy during World War I.

She had to sign for him to go. She didn't want him to go, he wanted to go. He enlisted but, he was only seventeen years old. But he liked that idea of the uniforms and all that and the travel. To see, travel and......
Ethel Waters used to go up there and dance her brains out.
And Louis and Ethel used to go up there and dance their brains out. Louis was a good dancer you know.

They would take old Jimmy Dorsey up there one night, yes. We were coming out of the Raxy Theater and he said, where are you going? And I said, we are going up to the Savoy to hear Count Basie. And then that's when we were leaving the next day for Europe. And old Count Basie say, you going to beat me over there? I say, I'm leaving
tomorrow. (LAUGHTER). Yes, this cut wanted to know if I was going to beat him over there. I said, I'm leaving tomorrow.
Well that was a, I mean there's another thing about it, you know, the way it was run. It was good wasn't it? I mean you had a big crowd but there was no nonsense.

The nonsense there was too much man. A lot of ex-fighters you know, as bouncers in that joint. And then if you got thrown out the last foot you felt was the doorman George ( right in the butt, you see. He didn't miss, you see because (?). Boy that was something. Everybody used to go there.
We'd go over Sunday night if you weren't working.
Well now, we are going back to the Navy. Your mother couldn't have liked that though could she?
Oh yes.
She did?
Sure.
I mean the War was on.
Yes, she wanted me, she wanted
me to do anything I wanted to. I was the most free. I had freedom. I didn't get no knocking around, kicking around or anything like that.
That's why I say he's spoiled. He was spoiled from a baby.
Well yes, but that's sometimes better than being kicked around too much.
Yes, that's right.
Yes, see it didn't leave him with a bad taste in his mouth. I think that's why he's been so nice all through the years.
You don't grow up with a chip on your shoulder.
No, no chip.
Well when you came out of the Navy then what happens now?
Then I started driving an automobile, for (Dr. Coca?).
Why did you do that?
That's what I wanted to do.
(LAUGHTER).
I didn't know anything else.
Well I mean was that the matter of a uniform again?
No, no uniform. I just wore

my cap. Yes I worked for (Bryant) and they had a big Cadillac and the kids, oh they loved me, you see. And my mother was really a professional cook. She was a chef you see, because I remember when we used to go, they called her Madame (Hendon Le Jeune).
How do you spell that? Hendon?
Yes.
What does that mean?
It's a big building in New Orleans by the name of the Hendon Building.
Oh, I see.

Looked like that was the name of her husband. Then I knew all the kids. The son's kids see, and she was sort of a, she was a grandmother. Madame Le Jeune. And she was always after me to go to school and finish up in New Orleans so she could send me to (Tuskegee). That's what she wanted because she thought that Booker T. Washington was the greatest educator in the world at that time, you know. And that's what she wanted me to do for mama, you know. She says, I just hope Zutty stay in school so I can send him to (Tuskegee) that's where I want him to go.
Well that was the right idea.
It sure was.
Yes, it was.
But maybe I wouldn't have got the other things.
Well that's right.
You see.
That's right, yes.
But I am so sorry that I didn't get the proper education. Very, very, very sorry. That has stopped me so much.

Well you know, it stops you in certain ways, but then on the other hand, you know, some people that have a lot of education they have been stumped in other ways. They don't know life, you know, I was talking to......

Always says, Alma always says if you have a degree you can sit down. She has one degree and now she's studying, she says she's going back in January, she has to make a few more points to get her Masters.
Now, I can't see it.
She wants those degrees.
This one guy, a professor,

from (Fisk?) University, he and his wife were in one night and I was telling, I was explaining my case to them about I didn't have the proper education. And she told me, she says, Zuddy the way you play them drums you don't need no education. Just keep on playing those drums like that. Now that's what this guy's wife told me.

Well you see it's perfectly true because if you had, if you had spent several years acquiring like a book education, an education out of books etc and etc., you probably would not have been the drummer you became. I really don't think you would.
Right.
Because you got a different outlook on life, you know?

In all my travels I was a loner in a way. Like in (Upper Twiss?) Open woods I used to go out in the woods by myself and things like that. Just with a stick you see and nothing ever happened to me. Just like when I went to Chicago the first time I got in a flat car with all that iron on me and went out to the .........
We haven't told this you know.
Oh?
No. Because we got this on the tape that got messed up. No we haven't done that yet.

The way I went up and asked the engineer, can I shovel coal to Chicago and things like that. And I walked through that yard where they had the toughest railroad detectives in the world. Walked right on through and nobody didn't say nothing. And things like that.

I tell Zutty that every day or every other day. That education would have meant one thing in fact the thing that's hurt him. Now I was going with Jerome Pascal when I first joined my brother's band he was a saxophone player.
Well is that where he came from, St. Louis?
Yes.
Sure.
He was with Fletcher wasn't he?
Do Cook too.
And he was my, what you would call, sweetheart. He was my sweetheart long before I met Zutty. Because when I first started playing with my brother's band Jerome was playing saxophone. I had

just finished highschool. He was finishing the next year. He was still going to highschool. And oh boy, I liked him because he was so clean and so quiet, so nice. And we went together for about two years. After he finished school he said he wanted to go to Chicago to study music to get a degree. Because after he went to Chicago he started playing with Doc Cook's band.
And we corresponded and we corresponded. Well he had no eyes for marriage at all. Because he wanted to get a degree in music. Well to make a long story short, he got a degree in music.
He went to the conservatory too in Boston.
Yes. He got his degree in music. When we come to New York, Zutty's still playing drums and Jerome is working in the Welfare Department.
After all that knowledge.

Well yes, but you see what that was. I mean so he, he was a well schooled musician but the kind of thing had sort of practically been drilled out of him, by that education. You know, I mean He'd become more like a classical musician really in his thinking don't you think?
Yes. He changed the way he
spelled his name. He felt like if he spelled it the Spanish way, from a Puerto Rican he wanted to become, to get work. Because the Puerto Ricans were getting all the work around New York.
He was very nice looking.

He was nice looking. But the last time I saw, he'd passed away. He passed away recently because I read it in the musician's thing. He was bald headed. Head just like Yul Brynner. As I said, he got his degree, but when we came back to New York he was working in the unemployment. No music, he couldn't get a job any place. And Zutty was still playing music.
Yes, but when you talk of education, Zutty, did you mean the general education? You didn't just mean music?
No I meant a general education.
That's right.

Well one thing, Zutty could read very well and write very well. See, because I would take care of his business and everything for him, I guess people were under the impression that Zutty couldn't write. Zutty writes fine. And he used to correspond, huh?
I did before this stroke.

Yes. And you still sign your checks because I don't sign them. He signs his own checks even with the stroke. I make him write sometimes. You write fine. And when he was, well people would get that impression that I mean Zutty couldn't read or write or something. He could write fine before he had this stroke and everything else.
What you really meant though was a fuller education, that's what you really meant? I mean you'd liked to have had a broader, I mean everybody ..... .
And he figures very well. Of course, like I heckle Zutty sometimes. I used to get mad and have to do everything he said, well you started it so you keep it up. You know, taking care of his business.
Just taking over.

And he'd say, you started it, so just keep it up. Because he couldn't attend to his business. I was so accustomed to doing it for Charlie and so I said well I'll do it. And then everyone got the impression that Zutty couldn't read and he couldn't write. Shoot, Zutty can read and write as good as I can. Maybe he couldn't write as good as
I can, because I could always write pretty well. But he could write very well. As well as Louis Armstrong. But Louis made a practice of writing and all that.
Oh yes, you mean when he was typing his letters?

And then he got so he wrote longhand you know, himself. I've always taken care of his business with the union, everything you know. Well I figure I don't have anything else to do, he's working. He likes to sleep during the day where I could get up and go you know. ( )piano player. I've always taken care of everything say like Lucile, take the rap. I've taken the rap.
Well you were doing that with your brother's band?
For my brother.
Sure.

And I was always making out all the contracts and everything. Well like Nick, Nick hadn't paid them for months down there. He just give them ten dollars a week or something like that. Business was bad, but I had my books that I kept how much he owed Zutty and the band you know. And finally, business
got better and he told Zutty he was going to straighten him up on Saturday night. So Zutty said alright, Marge will be up.
Nasty shock for (Nick) I'm sure.
(LAUGHTER).

And I had my books with me and I went down there you see. He and I sat down to the table. And I opened my books. He was going to give me so much money and I opened my books and told him. He say, hey you keep them books? I said, yes, I've been keeping books. And he told Zutty, he said, my goodness, he said we should have more wives like Margie. Margie is really taking care of your business. And I told him just how much he owed me.
Well did they agree?

Yes. Except I showed him these books and all. And a mess when we went to Europe when I was crying about my brother, but he hadn't given me the correct amount. Marg sure watches that money. I said, you're damn right, that's why she's with me. And I always went to the front for him, took care of everything. He fired Hank Duncan because Hank Duncan came on the job drunk.
Where was this?
At the Vanguard.
That's Nick's.
Nick's, this was in Nick's.
Oh, still in Nick's, yes.

And so Zutty came home and told me, he said I fired Hank tonight. I'm sick of him getting drunk. We couldn't play at all tonight. So I said, you fired him? Did you give him two weeks notice? He said, I fired him.

But what I'd like to say I had Edmund Hall was playing the clarinet too, we had a trio, see? So, old Hank would make the introduction in one key and then when he'd go to the chorus to start on the tune he'd change the key. And old Hall would say, man, what's the matter with you? You see, he was trouble (?).
Well he was drunk most of the time. Really drunk all the time. But a good piano player.
But he didn't really make the changes, did he, deliberately?
Yes.
But wasn't that partly because he was drunk?
I think so.
No, no, no. Not the way he did it. He'd make the introduction in one key and then when Hall would start to play he'd go to another key.

Well Zutty fired him and he came home and told me and said, well I let Hank go, I told him, I fired him tonight, I can't stand him no more. I said, you give him a two weeks notice? No, I told him don't come to work tomorrow night. I said, well you can't do that Zutty, you have to give him two weeks notice.

Well I did; shoot, I got my clothes on and went down to the union because I was going to pay the tax for the band anyway. I paid the tax every week for the band. And who did I meet but Hank Duncan. And he was glad to see me. He said I just put in charges against Zutty because he didn't give me two weeks notice. I said, oh no, you come to work tonight. I said, we changed that. I said no, I said you just be on the job tonight I said, because he didn't mean it, I said. So you don't have to file any charges. And he went in and took the charges out.

Yeah, really.
RAGTIME
He turned out to be the waltz king.
How extraordinary. Well, which boat were you on?
I was on the --
St. Paul.
It was the St. Paul.
St. Paul. And what was --
The other band, Jules Buffano, and them, they were on the JS. They have two boats, see, in St. Louis at the time. The JS, they got the society crowd, and the St. Paul got the ordinary --
JS. What did that stand for?
John Strickles, I guess.
John Strickles, oh, yeah.
Yeah.
The brothers, those Strickles Brothers knew music.
Yeah, yeah.
That's why Fate's band was the finest band ever heard in your life.
Well, this boat came from St. Louis to New Orleans?
In the summertime --
Yeah.
-- it was in St. Louis.
Hemlock
: Yeah.
: And in the wintertime the boat was the capital at that time, see, because the capital would go to St. Louis then we'd get off at the capital and transfer to St. Paul.
: Oh, I see.
: And then the capital would go around Iowa somewhere.
: Oh.
Well, how did these boats operate then. I mean, if you were in St. Louis on the St. Paul, would you be just doing excursions out of St. Louis?
: Yes, that's right.
: You wouldn't be going long trips on it.

: No, not long trips. Because see in the summer time, as I said, we were in St. Louis, and in the winter time we were in New Orleans. And they did the same things. They would go up or down the river for a while, see then finally we'd get back to dock about 11:30.
: Yeah.
: And see 12:00 o'clock we were off.
: What time would the boat leave in the evenings?
Well, around about 8:00 o'clock.
Oh, I see. So about four, three and a half hours.
Yeah. And that's when Little EVA Talbot, they used to come on board. He was a star football player at Tulane University, see, and he used to get us the -- to play at one of the frat houses.
Little Eva?
Little Eva Talbot because he was so large, you know.
Why did they call him Eva for?

I don't know. Little Eva Talbot, that was his name. And we'd go out to the frat houses, you know, and play, and sometime they'd only have 10 or 12 couples there. But he liked the music and oh, he was just crazy about us.
How big a band was the white Marable band when you joined it?
When I joined it they had three sax, banjo, you know, four rhythm.
Yeah.
And the trombone and two trumpets.
More or less the same as [Unintelligible]
And then they had a guy on violin and he doubled on horn, the peck horn.
Well, I take it that what you played, I mean it wasn't sort of out and out jazz all the time, you had to play --
No, it was really -- it was a different --
It was really like popular music.

It was different music. And we'd have rehearsals, you know, we'd get latest records and it was a certain things the captain wanted us to copy off the record. Because I remember how we used to do Ted Weems' sobbing blues. Plus we had little different parts in there. See, we'd get the orchestration, see then different parts in there, the captain wanted that copied like --
Yes, I see. And of course you would have to play the pop songs of the time, and you'd have to play I take it waltzes and everything.
Yeah, waltzes. We'd play beautiful waltzes, and all the latest tunes.
Yeah.
Well, when did you get the two pianists? You brought another pianist there in.
Well, they brought this piano --
Loving Good.
Loving Good. See, it was two pianists. He joined the band later.
He joined after you were there.
Yeah, after I was there, see.
Who was the other piano.
Loving Good.
Yeah. Who was the first one?
Fate Moralle.
Oh, Fate himself.
Yeah, Fate himself.
Well, who else was in the band when you joined it, famous. Anybody?
Well, Bert, Sydney, Desvignes, Desney, Amos White, and --
Well, I can check that out.
Louie had gone
Oh, yeah, Louie, in Chicago, I think.
Well, how long did you do this?
Oh, I put a couple of seasons on the board.
Yeah? And this when you met Marge for the first time?

That's right, that's when I first met Marge. Charlie Creath, I'd met her brother in Louisville, Kentucky. He came up for the Derby, and he invited me to come over to his home, when I got to St. Louis. And that's --
so I went over to his house after I got all straightened out, got located, and dressed all up and went over to his home. And Marge was on the floor shooting dice with the boys.
You mean with her brother Sam?
Yeah, because they'd had rehearsal that day. I think I told you this before.
Yes.
They'd had rehearsal and after rehearsal they had a little lunch, then after -- after they had lunch they would start card games, dice, things like that.
Yeah.
Yeah, I met Marge on her knees. She looked up at me and said, very glad to know you.
Was she playing piano in the band then?

Yes, she was playing piano in the band. Yes, she was playing good. A lot of guys in St. Louis would really brag on Marge, said, good piano player. And like Doc Randall, when I was playing at the Club 47 in California, Doc Randall, he was one of the owners of the place, he was a saxophone player. He's in Las Vegas now. And Nappy Lamar, and --
Nappy Lamar, the banjo player.
The banjo player, yeah. Well, they were the owners. Nanny Brenanni.
Yes.
Doc Randall. They were the owners.
Of what?
Of this Club 47.
Oh, in L.A.
Yeah.
Yeah, I see, yeah.

And Doc Randall used to say, Marge has got the best left hand that come in here, because Marge used to set in sing and play with us sometimes, you know. And he loved the way Marge played that bass you know, that walking bass, you know. That was real St. Louis style, you know.
We'll get to talk about that in a minute. We'll give you a little pause while you think up some other things. Well, Charlie truth though, he had a big reputation around then too.
Yes, he did. Yes, he did. He -- and he was a big man on Dago Hill.
On Dago Hill.
Yeah, that's a place where Yogi Berra and that bunch came from and all.
Well, was that like -- Dago Hill, was that a sort of an entertainment section?
No, not exactly, no. It was Italians, you know.
Oh, oh, I see. But they called it Dago Hill, you know.
Yeah, (inaudible).
Yeah, excuse the expression. But we used to go do a lot of work out there, and the Jewish people, they loved it. And you know how the black people loved it.
Yeah.
And at one time they started to have three or four bands working on one night, and he'd make the rounds to all the places.
Oh. Tell me, what sort of trumpet player was he? Did he use mutes quite a bit?

He played a lot of mutes, he loved mutes. And he just had a wonderful feeling for music, you know, because he had a lot of experience. He had been with P. G. Lowry's Lauries, Ringling Brothers band, marching band. He must have put about two seasons in on that. Yeah. He was -- got that circus training and everything, and very good musician and could play several instruments, you know. Oh, he was just a wonderful, wonderful guy.
How long did he -- what happened to him?
Well, when we were on our way to Europe we stopped to see him. We spent a whole night with him and it looked like he didn't want us to go out no place. So we
spent our time with him and when we got on the boat we received a telegram and they said Charlie was dead and everything. But we didn't know how.
And this would be when, Zutty?
This was 1951.
'51, yeah. How old would he be?
Well, Charlie -- oh, let's see. Well, never mind.
But what had he done in the meantime between that time when he died and when you --

Well, he had a bookie, see. That was causing the death, I think, because he had a bookie, Lodo and he, they were good pals, and they were running this bookie race horses, you know, and everything like that. And so Charlie were waiting for Lodo to come in and pay off a debt, like he was threatened or something, you know, to pay this debt off see. But Lodo didn't get in, so Charlie waited on him and waited on him and everything, and he never did show up with this bread.
Yeah.
So right after that, that's when Charlie committed suicide.
Oh.
Yeah, he committed suicide. Drank lysol and shot himself.
Oh it was the thought of the debt
that was worrying him. The debt, the fact that he couldn't pay off.
Yeah, that's right.
Oh, that's a shame.
That's what we always put it to. Because we received this telegram on the boat and said Charlie had died. But we didn't know about why and how until we got to Paris.
Right.
And that's when Charlie's wife wrote us a letter and explained everything.
Well, how long did -- we're talking about your brother now, how long --
How old was Charlie, Marge, when --
Now Charlie would be about 76.
Yeah.
So that was '51, it was 21 years ago. He was about 55.
Yeah.
Well, what I was -- you just have a rest since we've got to this period. What I was asking him was what did he do -- did he keep bands going for a long time or did he get out of music?
Well, he got out of music I guess -- we left St. Louis in '25, and I suppose he got out of music

I guess around '30 because he still kept going. So many musicians we meet now who worked with him, that we didn't know, you know, in St. Louis. Yeah. Shorty Charlie Baker worked with him. Well, Shorty Charlie Baker wasn't around when we were there.
No. He was just coming up.
He was just coming up. And several younger musicians that we --
Just like Willie Umphrey. He worked with Charlie.
Yeah, he worked with Charlie.
That was after we were there.
After we left St. Louis. So I think Charlie kept his bands going for about five years after we left there.
Now, what --
We went to Pittsburgh, we went through Pittsburgh because Charlie was playing on the boats in Pittsburgh.
Yeah, he was working on the boats, that's right. He had given up his band.
Yeah, but he was playing on the boats, he was playing on the boats.
Yeah, but I can't remember how --
And we looked for him that night and we couldn't find him --
Yeah, but we were on our way to New York.
Yeah.
Yeah, that was in '36. Because you had your new Ford.
That's right.

Yeah, they had a '36 Ford, we would drive into New York. We were coming through -- he had left the Three Deuces. Charlie had given his bands up and was working on a boat. That's why I said he had only been on the boat about a year.
What I wanted to ask you though was what was your music background, I mean what -- how had you -- I mean had you been trained as a pianist?

Yes, I had taken lessons, and I wanted to play rag time but I took lessons from a piano teacher who was teaching my sister, and my sister didn't have any talent for piano. I could play her exercises just by listening to them in the other room. So I had all the talent, and I took lessons for oh, about three years, and -- the Czerny method they called it.
Yeah.
Which everybody now -- the piano players now tell me what a good method that was.
Yeah.

I played house parties and all of that, just for my own pleasure and then I would learn rag time piano from Frank Eubanks, who learned it from Jelly Roll, and then he would teach me these rags, you know, and I would play house parties --
Jelly Roll had spent quite a bit of time in --
In St. Louis.
-- St. Louis.
He was playing in a nickelodeon there when I was going to high school.
Well, now what is the difference between East St. Louis and St. Louis. Is that --
It's a bridge, East St. Louis is across the East Bridge.
And East St. Louis is in Illinois.
Illinois, and St. Louis is in Missouri.
Yes.
It's just right across the bridge.

So when I finished high school I wasn't doing anything, and my sister was going to college. I didn't want to go to college, I didn't want to be a school teacher or anything like that, and it was so hard on my mother sending my sister to college, I didn't want nobody to work that hard for me. And so I went into nurse training, and I took

nurse training for two and a half years, had only a half a year to finish nurse training. And then I got mad with the supervisor of nurses, came home, and I wouldn't finish there. And they said if I would come back and apologize to the supervisor, you know, I could go back in. I only had six more months to finish. And I wasn't going to apologize to anybody, I was a young militant, I guess.
An early one.
(Inaudible).

Yeah, a real early militant because I just wasn't going to bow down for anything. So then my brother said -- he told my mother I had to do something, and he wasn't going to have me hanging around doing nothing and he was going to put me to work playing piano, and I cried. With his band. Oh, I cried. I couldn't play that good, he said well you're going to play, you're going to practice and you're going to play. You don't want to do anything, you've got to work, you've got to help mama. So he put me to work and I could read. In those days you had to read the orchestrations. (Unintelligible) as good as all piano players, and so I worked with him and his dance band. The first job I had was playing at the dance hall called Almac in St. Louis.
Almac?
ALMAC, A-l-m-a-c. Almac dance hall.
He put me to work in the band and he said play, you're going to play, take the music and just play with the band. And I played
with the band, and boy, the time I was crying and --
How old were you?
I was 19.
Oh, yeah, uh-huh.

18, 19, because I had been out of high school. Still not 20 because I'd been out of high school hanging around there, didn't know what I wanted to do. But I didn't want to go to college, I know that. I didn't want -- not that I didn't love school and all, but my mother had to work too hard. So my first job was playing with the band, which was just about six pieces; trombone, saxophone, trumpet, piano, drums and guitar. That was the instrumentation. And boy they played like mad, and then finally the band got so good everybody loved it, so Charlie wanted a name for it. What are we going to name it. So we rehearsed -- and the boys were happy with me, they said I played good. The most they wanted was accompaniment, they didn't care whether it was a lot of executions, as long as I played the right notes and the right tempo.
Yeah.
And then Charlie said jazz was coming in and jazz --
Well, what sort of music were you playing then before, sort of dance music, popular?
Before (Unintelligible)?
No, you say jazz was coming in.

Well, we didn't call it jazz. It was jazz but they didn't call it -- they called it jazz. Then we started to call it jazz and Charlie said now they have a name for the band. And finally he came up with the name Jazz O'maniacs. That was the name of our band.
Charlie Creath.
Charlie Cramp and his Jazz O'Maniacs.

And then this was a colored dance hall, but these Italian boys and all around St. Louis started to hear about this jazz and they started to come into this dance hall 'cause they could dance by this music. And boy, we had as many white as blacks. They almost took it over because they loved that music. And Charlie was reading about jazz, jazz, jazz, you know, they called it jazz o'maniacs. That was the name -- and we rehearsed every week, once a week, and from then on why the Italian boys started to want to hire Charlie for their dances.
And did they -- up from Dago Hill.

From Dago Hill. And they wanted -- and there was the first white place we played was a hall on Pine Street -- I've forgotten the name of it but that was -- these Italian boys, some of their friends owned this band so they got them to hire Charlie's band 'cause they'd had always white bands.
Was that the Arcadian?

No, no, the Arcadian was like Roselord, and we were the first black band to play. They got Charlie to play at this hall on Pine Street. That's where it was -- in those days it was segregation, it wasn't integrated. It was all white at this dance hall, and that's where Jack Bland and --
Dick Slevin.
Dick Slevin. They used to -- they were bell hops, they loved music --
And none other than Red --
McKenzie?
Red McKenzie.
Was he from St. Louis?
Sure, and he was hopping bells at the Marquette Hotel.
What hotel?
The Marquette.
Oh, yeah.
And they came out there and heard the band and from then on they were coming in with these clothes combs and things, asking to play with the band. They played with the band.
Sat in.
Yeah.
They were the Mound City Blue Blowers.
Hemlock

Yeah, they formed it after they got getting their rehearsals with Charlie, and boy Charlie was so hot. We'd be playing good and Charlie cursed all the time, you know. Here come them son of a b's with them combs. Oh, goddamn it. You got to be worried with them. But you know, he'd GREET them, and oh, they'd start blowing with the band and this Coleman. And one of them had a banjo --
Yeah, that was Dick Slevin.
Yeah, he played the banjo.
(Inaudible).

Yeah, and Jack Bland, and it was a natural drug to (unintelligible) Charlie, but he wouldn't let on to them, you know, and that's where they got after -- for a few years that's when they become the Mound City Blue Boys. They got their experience -- they were hopping bells. They couldn't play any place.
Yeah, yeah.
And they played with Charlie and that's where they --
Frankie Tromban made his records with them.
Yeah.
The Mound City Blue Blowers.
Well, now, Frankie was from St. Louis?
Yeah.
(Inaudible).
Well, what were they doing at this time?
The Frankie Trumbauer was a society band.
Oh.

And he heard about Charlie, and he came to hear the band, and he was playing at the place called -- well, he was at the Arcadia, and he told a man -- it was a place just like Roseland, a beautiful ballroom. Never thought of hiring a black band but Frankie Trumbauer wanted this boss to have Charlie to come in there for one night, see. And I'll never forget, because I had to buy a gown, oh, and they bought tuxedos, the band dressed up in tuxedos. We were sharp when we went there and broke it up. And from then on, different people started calling Charlie, could he play parties for them. And then from -- after meeting Frankie Trumbauer, he played in the summer time at a place called West Lake, and Ted Jansen, Pee Wee, and I don't know, a gang of musicians were playing.
Ted Jansen. (Inaudible).
He was a good drummer he had drummer
And Charlie --
What?
Ted Jansen.
Jansen.
He owned the band.
Oh, I see.
His band and trombone -- Thumbauer was...
Sonny Lee was one, and Bix, and--
Bix was there then?
Sure.
And Sonny Lee I called it, and -- but the piano player (inaudible).
We never could remember. He was a terrific --
I can't remember his name. He was on the order of Rag time Joe Wrightman.
Yeah, he was on the Wrightman style. And Zuddy I always wondered if he was --
And (inaudible).
He could have been Joe Wrightman, Zuddy, we never did get straight on that. But he was terrific.

But I think that was the first mixed band I ever played with because Charlie was going to play this benefit for Bob Russell. He was a Negro producer, you know, and they were giving a big thing at the Booker Washington Theatre. That was right in the section, you know. And so Charlie said to me, said I think I'll ask these old boys, say go up and play this benefit with us, see because we were playing at West Lake, see, alternating like, you know, two
bands.
Yeah, we were doing that when Zutty came to St. Louis. But we had done it long before you came there, you know.
Oh, yeah.

Well, this night -- any way, Charlie asked me do you I think I'd better ask these boys to go up and play this benefit for us, with us, see. So he asked one of the guys, and he said, sure, let's go, let's go. And we went up to this Booker Washington Theatre and when that curtain went up and they saw that band mixed --
Yeah.
-- boy what a hand. I never will forget that hand we got that night.
Which were the guys then that played? The Trombar. Trumpauer?
That played with the mixed band?
Yeah.
No, this was when we went up to play at the Booker Washington Theatre. Charlie asked these guys would they come up and join together.
But we had the white band, Pee Wee Russell was one.
Yeah, Pee Wee Russell.
But Trombar didn't go, did he? Trumpauer
Trumbauer
I don't know if Trombar was there --
There were several other boys --
And more sure Moshelle Bix was there, and Sonny Lee, the trombone player. That was just a grand thing.
Yeah, it must have been.
It really was. Man, I think that was the first mixed band I ever played in. I knew it was.
Yes. Well, when Zutty comes to St. Louis, with professional destiny laid out --

That's right, that's right. But to tell you how Charlie got started, and then so many people wanted his music, all the whites, you know what I mean, and the blacks. They'd heard about Charlie Nick come to hear him (unintelligible) until he couldn't -- our band couldn't play for these different engagements, but he'd tell them he would get them a band.
Yes, I see.

And then he would appear for one number or something, because we always had two or three gigs on the same -- I mean, you know, he'd hire. But he didn't turn down any gigs because there were too many musicians around there that were good that he could hire them and he would make one appearance at these different places.
Yes, I see.
And then I'd --
So he was really the star musician there then.
Yeah.
He was a poor man's Myer Davis.
Yeah.
Yeah, I see.
See, and then his band was getting better and better, and --
But how outstanding was he as a trumpet player?

That's what I'm telling you. If he just played one number per dance the people were happy. He was -- they thought he was the greatest trumpet player in the world. They didn't think about -- in those days folks didn't think about Louie Armstrong, it was Charlie Creth.
Charlie Creth.

Charlie Creth. And the whites -- they wouldn't call it Creth they called it Charlie Creth C-r-e-a-p-h, but it was pronounced Creth, the /a/ was silent. And then the band -- I started taking care of all of his business, I really took care of all the contracts, hiring the boys, you know, find out how many pieces they wanted. Because all the time Charlie was a gambler at heart, he loved to gamble.
That runs in the family.

Yeah, he loved to gamble. And so he could leave it to me -- I checked his books and I could find out how many pieces they wanted, and give them a price, and said tell them how much deposit they had to send in before I sent the contract to them. They'd get on the phone and hire different musicians, maybe four pieces, maybe five pieces, no more than six pieces.
Well, now, how did you come into this picture, Zutty? You'd met him before?
No.
No, I hadn't met him until we were on our way to St. Louis --
Oh, I see.
And we had to stop off in Louisville and play a Louisville ball that night, a derby ball. See.
Yeah. This is Fate Marable's band.
This is Fate Marable's band, right.

And Charlie invited me to his home when I got to St. Louis, and after I got straight and all I went up to see Charlie, and then that's when I told you I met Marge. She was shooting dice down on the floor. She looked up at me and said, very nice to meet you.
Was it love at first sight, or did it develop?
It must have been.

It must have been because I told Zutty, when I looked up from shooting dice, I looked in his face, something hit me. But to get back to the boats, after -- before Charlie started forming all these bands and things, they hired him for a season on the St. Paul.
Oh.

And he brought me, and they were not going to have me, these Streckfuss Brothers, because they were accustomed to that good piano that Fate Marable was playing. And then these piano players in Isham Jones and Buffanos, they were real piano players. And they wanted 'Kitten' on the keys, and I didn't play that too good. It was pretty difficult. But any way, they told Charlie they didn't want me, and so Charlie said if you don't want her you don't want my band. So if you hire me you have to have her, and I'll take care of my music. So they hired me but they said they didn't want to do it, but afterwards they all liked me so much. (Lacks) and Captain John and all.
Captain Vernon.
Captain Vernon. They all liked me so much.
Captain Joe (inaudible).
And the band made such a hit on the boat. But I was not featured like Fate, but Charlie was.
Yes, he was --

He was the man, see he was the king, you know. Did the whole season on the St. Paul and took it to dry dock in Iowa with Charlie, so then when we came back to St. Louis that's when the work first started, just coming in. I hadn't even met Zutty then. Because Zutty wasn't on the boat, I was on the boat before Zutty. I met Louie Armstrong on the boat, not just -- he played with Fate Marable's band, we'd go on there on Monday night, and Louie Armstrong was so shy he'd jump over that bandstand and run downstairs to the water fountain trying to get away from the girls, you know. And I wanted to talk with him because Charlie was a trumpet player, too, you know, and so I introduced myself to him that I was Charlie's sister, you know, and all, and he just kept his head down.
He was collecting gum wrappers then. He used to have a coupon on the back of a package of gum, and that's what he was looking for, and that's--
But that's where I met him.

But when he first came to St. Louis they had a bottle of olives, see, and when he got off of the train why this bottle slipped and these olives started to rolling all over the station floor, and he tried to pick each one up.
It was really a sort of very unique
experience at this time.
But when I met Zutty I had been with Charlie's band for about four years, you know, and --
I was asking Zutty while you were on the phone, your brother was a big man with mutes, wasn't he?
Yes.
Well, now, King Oliver -- I mean had he -- were he and King Oliver friends or --
No.
No?
No, he didn't know anything about King Oliver. Charlie had his experience with the P.G. Lowry. That's where he got -- see he left home when he was 17 years old and he joined the circus.
Yeah.
What was the name, was it --
Ringling?

Ringling Brothers Circus, in the side show. And P.G. Lowry was a concert musician. He really could blow the trumpet, and Charlie -- remember of course Charlie had his first experience in a high school band in St. Louis under Professor Bowles. That's where he learned how to read, how to blow. And my older brother played trumpet.
Oh?
But Charlie played clarinet.
What happened to the older brother?

He died when he was 17 from scarlet fever, and they didn't know what it was. But he was supposed to be very great, you know, and he went the country with my grandmother, and they sent for my mother, and he was dead, practically, when she got there. But after he passed away Charlie took the trumpet, that's what he wanted to blow any way, but he could really blow clarinet.
Yeah?

Oh, yeah. He was a musician. Believe me he was a musician. He played piano, he could read anything. He could read anything. If a saxophone player was wrong or something he'd go and show him like where he worked.
I see.
Any of the instruments.
That's why he had a good band.

Yes, he was -- but Charlie took the trumpet, and 17 -- because it broke my mother's heart. She always wanted us to go to college, you know, she always wanted us to have a good education, she said, because she didn't that's why she had to work so hard. Charlie left and joined the circus under PG Lowary, and we have a picture of him in the circus band.
Oh, really?
Yes. And he was second trumpet in
that band, and that's when he came back home and he was really blowing. Charlie had been half way around the country before he was 21.
Well, what other -- were there any other good trumpet players in St. Louis?
There were, but people didn't consider them.
No.
There was Eddy Allen, --
Dewey George Jackson.
-- George Jackson. They tried to --
(Inaudible).
They tried to have bands and the people really didn't want them, they wanted Charlie.
Well, they weren't as good musicians as Charlie, though, were they?
Oh, they were good musicians.
No, as good.
Oh, maybe not, but St. Louis was noted for good musicians.
Now, see, they came up in the Masonic band.
They really were.
They all read music, all of them.
Oh.

That was a must in St. Louis then, you understand what I mean, you had to read, you know, because Old Man Langford, Harvey Langford's father, he was a great trombone player too. He was in the circus too, but Old Man Langford had a band under one of the largest, the Masonics.
The Masonics.
Yeah. And these young boys, he trained them in all these -- all the young musicians in St. Louis came up under Langford.
Well, this is really the secret of it, really a good ______.

Sure, sure. The same with Clark Terry. Now Clark Terry came up after we left St. Louis but how he admired he told me, I had my Charlie when he was young. That's why Clark Terry's such a good musician in St. Louis. I mean, you know --
And Shorty Baker too.
Shorty Baker, oh, yeah. But Clark Terry, he never worked under Charlie but Shorty Baker did.
Yeah. I mean, Shorty, he was a fine trumpet.
Yeah. And Irving Randolph. Now he's out of the business. Ham Davis, Leonard Davis. He's dead, they called him Ham. Oh, we had so many musicians.
Yeah, it was like a real school.
