And Nick told me he says, I don't like that fish horn. Get that fish horn out of here. Say I don't like it. So finally, (Bashey?) and the Spirits of Rhythm and myself we went back into Nick's. And of course old Nick had found out just who (Bashey?) was, see? Because at that time old (Bashey?) had him a pressing shop. He wasn't doing nothing you know. And boy, we got back in there and he'd come up to our house and talk about the Spirits of Rhythm. How he wanted to .....
I said, get him out of there.
Wanted to get like, worried Margie to death see?
The spirituals.
He called them the spirituals.

The spirituals. And wanted Zutty to go to the union with him and to put a knock in against them that they weren't acting right. They were getting drunk and all, get them out. And Zutty said I'm not going to tear up the group.

Finally, after all of this going on, Nick tells me one night, he say, Zutty, he say, the old man say he can't get along with you. And old Bechet and I hadn't had any trouble or anything like that. But he just wanted me out after me getting him in there.
Who wanted you out, Bechet?
Bechet.
Why?
So he could be the star.
Oh yes, yes. And Zutty had given him an overcoat and we were giving him breakfast every day and dinner. I didn't have to fix breakfast for Zutty.
Well this is the thing you know. I've heard that he was kind of mean.
He was.
Oh he was a mean cat, boy.
Yes, isn't that strange.
He wrote me a letter in Paris while we were there and I wish you could have seen all the dope
He said he wrote the letter to the Alvin Hotel because he was coming there to work across the street.
Well that's right.
He moved into the Alvin Hotel and he wanted you to be with his group. He was going to open across the street in the Band Box.
Yes, that's right.
Downstairs next to Birdland?
Yes.
And I was so mad when I read the letter, I got so mad I tore it up and threw it in the waste basket.
Yes boy, because he had so many debts.

And he was going to do some travelling and told Zutty how much poundage he would pay for on the airplane and the rest he would have to pay. And no drinking on the bandstand. And no drinking and I don't know what all. And all the don't. Don't do.........
Oh, I see. It was a real .....
A boss man?
Oh, he was a boss man.
(Unintelligible)
and Zutty said, you should have seen that letter.
I should have really kept that letter just to show...
It was unbelievable.
The things he wanted me to do.
When he did come Zutty told him he wasn't even thinking about working over there. But he flopped over there.

Yes. But you know what you were saying about Tommy Ladnier getting sort of discouraged. Well I mean there was a period in the thirties, now I can remember people used to say that Sidney Becket that's terrible that broad vibrato, That's corny. There was definitely a period of that because Helen made two records when she was working for Mills. They were the first records he was featured on for years. You know he was with Noble Sissle for a time.
That's right, Noble Sissle.
He didn't need anything though. You know, I mean.....
That's the way Nick could see it. Nick called it a fish horn.
Yes, yes.
And Zutty got him in, but he got Zutty out.
Got me out.
Zutty was feeding him. He had to have an overcoat. It was so cold.
I give him my overcoat.
It was so cold and he didn't have an overcoat.
It's extraordinary to think he would, was down that far, you know, isn't it?

He didn't have an overcoat and it was cold. He would come up to the house with his suit coat you know and that's when Zutty said, I'm going to give him an overcoat. And then Zutty come home and tell me what (Buckey) Becket wanted for his breakfast. He wanted some lost bread, which is with his French toast. I said, I don't fix breakfast for you and here you got me fixing breakfast for him. And I told Zutty, you just
wait, you'll see.
I had a lot of respect for him.

Oh he had so much respect. But I could almost see these things. I told Zutty just you wait, you watch and see if he appreciates all this you're doing for him. And Zutty said, oh Marge, you shouldn't be like that. I said, well I'm like that. I don't have to fix breakfast for you why............ Then he started bringing him for dinner. (LAUGHTER). And I never forget, one day I had a dinner ready and here he comes with some corn that I had to shuck. He saw some corn that he wanted along with his dinner and I had to stop and shuck it and cook it. But I couldn't tell Zutty anything. No, he's my boy. I have to look out for him.
One night it was so cold at Nick's I hid the overcoat that I gave him.
Because he was acting so nasty.
Yes. So bad, you know. And when I came out of Nick's he was standing there so cold so I went back in Nick's and got the overcoat.
And gave it back to him.
And gave it back to him.
Well was he, was he sort of a moody person or was he sort of really like this all the time? I mean, I've heard he's a kind of hard one.
Well you couldn't trust him.
Oh, was that it?
He was the type of guy .....
You couldn't trust him anyway.
Was he a selfish cat then?
Yes.
Yes, very selfish.
Very selfish. Oh very. And I told Zutty that. But Zutty didn't think that at all.

But Zutty didn't know when we went to France. Oh he was so glad to see us. We were one of the few people that he had out to his villa you know. Because everybody, even the French ones, that's an honor because he has nobody out there. He doesn't invite anybody, he doesn't care who comes from America. He had us out there.
He sure did.
Yes sir. He came and got us in his car, his special built.......
That was in Lille wasn't it?
Yes, he was married to a girl named Mills.
No, I said, Lille.
Lille, in France, yes.
LilArmstrong was with us.
Yes, was with us, yes. He invited the three of us. Yes, but ...............
And he was going in for fishing you know. And cameras, boy he had some of the most expensive cameras.
This is by the time he'd made it in France?
Oh he was the King. He was the King. He had this special built car with a soprano saxophone all over the front of it.
Where was he?
In Paris.
But where was the soprano?
On top of the hood. Right at the, on the hood.
Really?
Yes. And the horn, it would blow like a saxophone.
It would blow a riff like (Becket).
Oh you mean instead of a hooter?
Yes.
Really?
Sure. A special built Bentley wasn't it?
No, it wasn't. I don't know. I can't remember.
It was an English car. And he had it.....
It was one of those fine...... ....
Oh, it could be a Bentley. You know, it's a Rolls Royce with a different ............ ....
And he always wanted to take us out. And oh boy, he was, he really couldn't get over it he said, because you know he's such a big man and didn't associate with anybody.

I think it's very funny you know. One year Duke was playing up in Boston at that place of George Weins in the Bradford Hotel I think it was. And Paul Gonsalves said to me, with Zutty as I see it now as I begin to know more, that you may very

be deceived by the character of a person, but you love their music. So that's it for you. I mean the person might even be rotten, but if he can play like an angel then you are on his side. Well that's a good way to be in music really.
The only way.

And Zutty has always done that all his life. Color didn't make any difference, to him. He wasn't thinking of that like these militants. He loved the white ones as much as he loved the black boys. If they could play, if they were his friends, they were his friends.
And a lot of times I've said things and he said, oh Marge, don't be like that, he's a nice boy. Yes, don't be like that, he's nice.
Well that's the way to be really.

And that's the way he's been and he had so many knocks from them same ones that he has upheld. They didn't know it, the love that Zutty had in his heart for them. As I say, he never was an Uncle Tom or anything, but he loved his, he got Mel Powell started.
Really?

I don't think Mel Powell has said anything But Zutty's the one that got Mel Powell started and wanted Mel Powell to play with him at Nick's. And Nick didn't like the idea of a white boy playing with a black boy. And Zutty told him, said he can play the piano man. But Zutty had to get a black piano player. He wouldn't let Mel play with the outfit.
He let him play one night.
One night and Zutty said..
He said, man, he said, my customers wont like that. I said, okay. I said, no Nick, it's not your customers, it's you.
That's right.
That's what I told him.
And that's why I say, Mel's father gave Zutty a watch and they had us at their home for dinner.
Mel Epstien.
Yes, Mel Epstien. And they were so crazy about Zutty because they told Zutty you know, how kind he had been and all. And nobody else would listen to Mel, to Mel as a jazz piano player.
But Zuttv did.

The piano player that I always liked in Chicago, a white piano player was Jess Stacey. I always thought he was great. I still think he's great. You know. But he must have just got discouraged and fed up with it.
That's it. You know, I mean after all.....
When they find out they can go by themselves, they put it down. See, just like old Joe Sullivan, he did the same thing.

He became a loner. Didn't want to be bothered with anybody. He sent us a telegram when he found out Zutty was coming to Berkeley and he had everything arranged, he just wanted the three of us to be together, to hang out together. But Zutty had too many friends out there.
I had (UNINTELLIGIBLE), he and his wife. We had (Jackie Marlin?) he and his girlfriend were coming out there. And I just couldn't do it.
No, no.
Well he was a loner and didn't
want us to bother with anybody.
He was just going to take us out on the town. And so I didn't call him up while we were there. Because I couldn't, it was impossible for me to do it.

Now like this little English drummer, he was here, I've forgotten his name now, but he's made it big. He's done good anymore. But he would come into Ryans all the time you know, he loved Zully so. And he'd been corresponding with Zully from England before he came here. But anyway, one night Zully came home and said, what's his name, I can't think of his name. But anyway Zully said he was going to New Orleans and he said, Marge I gave him ten dollars because he looked like he's kind of beat. Now why did you give him ten dollars. Why didn't you let one of the other boys give him ten dollars, why did he want to lay on you? Zully said, Marge he didn't lay on me. He didn't ask me for it, I gave it to him because I felt sorry. And you shouldn't feel like that. What difference does it make? He's a nice boy. And I wanted to help him, he needs help and I knew he needed it, but he didn't ask for it. But I gave him ten dollars because he's going to New Orleans.
And do you know that boy, it wasn't but the year before last when Zutty first got the stroke, he sent a telegram and said he was having a benefit for Zutty in Frankfurt, Germany.
Oh yes? I wonder who he is now?
But I have the bill and everything. And do you know about two weeks later he sent Zutty a check for almost five hundred dollars.
Well that's the way you should do.
So Zutty said, well you see Marge?
You cast your bread on the waters?
Yes, so you see, I told you he was a nice boy. And he just heard about Zutty having this stroke. And he promoted this benefit in Frankfurt, Germany.
They had a lot of bands there.
They had a lot of bands there. I've got to look up that. I'll let you know the next time you come what his name is.
We should.....
Yes, that's what I mean he did. That's what he did.
Boy those names, you can forget them.
We know so many people.

I mean you see it's the difference of the professional musicians' life, but a person who say has the store across the street I mean he knows a limited number of people. But when you travel as you do and you meet people all over the World and when you've had a long career like yours, I mean, you know. People come in a club and they met you in Wisconsin fifty years ago. They remember you. They see you sitting up there behind the drums but what have you got to remember them by?
I mean, you might remember their face, but you couldn't remember their name. I think that's one of the hardest things that name business.

And Zutty used to, that's what Louis Armstrong said. He said, I never saw anybody with a memory like Zutty. He says, anybody comes up and says anything he says, yes, how are you Mr. So and So. He says he remembers names..........
Like he picks out a hard one. So old Louis said, well hello Bartholomews.
He said, how can Zutty remember all the names?
He said, I haven't seen the guy in so long. And I told him, I said, the last time we were
talking you know. I was telling him that I haven't got that memory any more like I used to have.
But his memory is better than mine.

I think his memory is great. I do think that there comes a point where I guess your memory absorb so much and then it begins, the new things that come in sort of tend to push out some of the old things you know?

But Zuddy can come up with things at night when we're sitting here. Don't you remember, and I say, no I don't remember that. And it will come to me in a couple of days, you know, who it was that he was talking about.

What we've done today actually, we've done, now we've done, we really started this in St. Louis you see. And we've done Chicago and we've come to New York. And he says, oh then you were with Pike Davis band backed Bill Robinson. Pike Davis band and you backed Bill Robinson.
Oh yes. Well that was in the La Fayette Theater.
Oh that was in the La Fayette?

Yes. That's when old Bill Robinson was would do a step,see, and I/supposed to make the make the things after him. And then that went on and on. And finally, he made such a terrific step that I just falls all through the drums, you know? And boy what a ......
Oh you really set him up?
Yes.
And Zutty has to tell you about the set up he had for Zutty to travel with him about the base ball game.

Oh yes. He had me all set up. I had my band together. Otto, Big Green, Bubber Miley and the whole band. And old Bill Robinson was a big man with the Yankees. You see, and he had charge of the black Yankees, see? So, ....
What do you mean? There were white Yankess and black Yankees?
Yes.
Oh, I didn't know.
Yes. Yes, well sure he did. Well anyway, the black Yankees were playing and he wanted me to bring a band up you know, so he could dance.
At the Yankee Stadium.

At the Yankee Stadium so he could dance on the dugout and everything you see? So man, I had a nice group out there you see. And so old Bill Robinson, it looked like he wasn't going to pay me for that you know? On the strength that he was taking me out on the road you see?

So man, I found that cat up in the office in the Yankee Stadium. And he said, nigger let me know what you want? I said, 'I want to get paid for today.' I said 'I've got a lot of good men out there.' I said, 'now me, I don't care if you pay me or not.' I said, 'but you've got to pay the other guys, see?'
So man, he raised hell. Oh he gave me hell. You see, but this job I was supposed to get, he gave it to Cab Calloway. Cab Calloway got that job.
Yes, because he told Zutty he said, I'm fixing to take you out on the road and all of that.
Yes. He said, I'm fixing to take you out on the road.
Oh Zutty, he caught it. It was the same with Joe Glaser when he was going to put Zutty in the Armstrong band. Zutty asked for the
same money that Cozy was getting. And Joe told him, don't be a horses ass.
Yes, that's what he said.
And he never did hire Zutty.

That's what he told me. He said, Cozy (Caucsey?) been with us seven years. I said, man, I don't care how long he's been with you. I said, I want the same amount of money that Cozy (Caucsey?) gets. (LAUGHTER).
Because Zutty wasn't worried, he was doing alright.
Yes, I was working with Wilbur DeParis at the time I met Jimmy Ryans.
But see Louis..........

Louis asked me, he said, how do you get along with Pops? I said, I get along fine with him. I said, we've never had one cross word in our life. And then I told him the little thing that happened at the Lenox Club that night. The night we'd taken May McKinney?) out to the after hours place. And Rex Stewart boy, he wanted to get to Louis, you know. And he got up on the stand and tried to hit a high note and he missed it and I hollered. And old Louis said, "look out there face. A little professional courtesy." (LAUGHTER). Yes, that's what he told me. Because old Rex was really
after him that night.
Zutty came home and told me Joe Glazer said, 'don't be a horses ass.'
Oh because you asked for the same money ?
Yes, yes.
As (Cozy)?
As (Cozy), yes.
Well what made him think you'd get the same as (Cozy)? For Heaven's sake.
Well that's what he told Zutty and they never did call Zutty. And Louis didn't stick up for Zutty.
Well I mean, you know, that was, that was..........
But Louis said he didn't want nothing to do with the business.
No, but I mean that was all, always rather ridiculous for Louis to have people like he did have on drums. I mean that was stupid.
I don't know who they got after that. Who did they get after that?
Well they had that (Deems Barrett Digs?) and .......
Barrett Deems, yes.
And they had Danny Barcelona.
And they had that other kid, what was that other little kid. Used to have his drums so loose.
I don't know, you mean after ............
John, Johns? (Rummy Johns)

Oh yes for a time, that's right. There was somebody, I never really heard them in person but I remember, yes. Well I mean that was a thing you know that Earl was telling me when he, I mean Earl Himes went.......... Yes, why did you go back to Chicago?
Well, now what time?

Well in the early thirties you played with the Berry Brothers dancing act. Then you were with Pike Davis backing Bill Robinson. We talked about Bill Robinson. And then it says you went on tour accompanying Norman and Arlene Selby, that's out of order there. Your show ended its run in Chicago when you were with Norman and Arlene Selby.
The place, the fair opened up, during that time. And this was, we were playing at the Follies Bergere.
Right, we've had that, didn't we?
Yes.
It says you settled in Chicago for several years, worked briefly with Jimmy Bell then rejoined Carroll Dickerson at the Grand Terrace in 1934. Is that right?
No. That can't be right. In '34?
And then it says later led own band at the New Deal Club. Then again worked for Dickerson. In may 1935 began leading own sextet at the Three Deuces.
Well that's true. That's right. But I didn't go back with Carroll Dickerson.
Not at all?
No. I don't remember that. Because he, the last time I played with Carroll Dickerson was when we came here to New York in '29. We were at Conrey's Inn. That's when Louis quit the band.
Well then was the Three Deuces next then? What about this New Deal Club he mentions?
Oh the New Deal, that was just a little joint over on the West Side. They had a lot of gangsters sons who would come in. And I even had Marge come over one night to play the piano for me.
Oh really?

Yes, because the piano player didn't show up or anything and I had to 'phone Marge up and ask her to come over and play. And her finger nails were so long, she sure did suffer that night. But she would do anything to help me you know? And they had this New Deal, they had a football game, a football team they were sponsoring you know? And boy they were the roughest young cats I ever saw in my life.

And every Friday night it was fish and chips, see, and old Charlie, Charlie was his name, ran the joint. And that was some place, believe me. (LAUGHTER). I had the Adam Brothers over there and Reuben Red Reeves.
Oh yes?
He played several nights over there with us.
Yes he was, he was from the Missourians wasn't he?
Yes. He was a good trumpet player, mdr.
And then after that did you go into The Three Deuces?
Yes, after that.
Yes. How long were you there?
Well I was there, oh, until about '37.
Yes?

Yes. And Art Tatum had taken the band over and I had been with Roy in The Three Deuces. See after it was my band first. Zutty and his band. See, then Roy came in because Roy was in town with Fletcher Henderson and he used to come down and sit in and everything. And finally, they had (break in?) from the Chicago River. And we came to work one night and the dance floor was floating. See, and so right after that we reopened and that's when (Sam Day?) hired Roy Eldridge.
I see.
See, and we had Truck Parham on bass.
And did Roy have his brother Joe over there? Did Roy have his brother working there?
Oh yes, yes.
Well when did you have that band that made that number 'Runende Papa' etc? Was that before Roy?
Yes, that was before Roy.
Oh, I see.
That was before Roy.
That was at The Three Deuces?
Yes it was at The Three Deuces.
And what was the band?
Dave Akappin, Dave Akappin. Had us to come and make that.
Yes.
Yes.

AN INTERVIEW WITH
MR. & MRS. ZUTTY SINGLETON
BY
MR. DANCE
SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION
PERFORMING ARTS
L'ENFANT PLAZA
AMTRAK BUILDING
(REELS 4, 5 AND 6)
When you went to Chicago then, part of it was that you wanted to see the World's Fair? Part of it, and also I take it because there were all these guys from New Orleans there?
Oh there were so many New Orleans guys in Chicago at the time.

Well then when you get there you have a period to wait because of the union? And then you go to that, we've got that on here when you worked at what's the name of the place, Jerry's / ? (Kelly's ?)........
(Kelly's Stable?)?
(Kelly's Stable?).

Well you didn't say too much about (Kelly's?). You really, what you really get to here is the Roulette band. And then you started to say, but we haven't got that on there that Doc Cook came and took you
Yes, yes. Doc took me and Butler and I.......
What did Butler play?
He was a saxophone player.
Oh, yes.
He was a fine saxophone player.
He's still around New York.
Oh yes?
He's in city work. He has some kind of.......
What's his first name? Oh, well never mind.
Well his name should be in there because.......
Yes it will be in the discography books.
It has to be Billy Butler.
Billy? Billy Butler. He's more white than black.
Yes?
Yes. And now I read about him in the Amsterdam News occasionally. He has a big city job.
King Oliver had him, had him
to direct his band at one time.
Really?
Yes.
He was a good musician?
Oh, he was a very fine musician. Very high class.
I know somebody called Jack O'Brian. And Freddy himself might have called him because Freddy's still around. She was married to Johnny Hodges.
The one thing though I think that was interesting which we should put on there about your trip up. You took two or three days and you had trouble with the generator?
Yes.
And you also packed the car.
That was on a different trip.
Oh.
A different trip. That was with Charlie.....
A different trip, but I mean we were leaving St. Louis for good then when we had the generator trouble.
We were in the cracker box.
(LAUGHTER).
But when I ran into the cows crossing the street, I must have dozed off or something. I was driving. And that was the old Peerless.
Was it the Peerless?

A big red car. A great big car because we were sleeping in the back of the car and Charlie was driving. And so Charlie got so tired he said to Zutty, Zutty you want to take the wheel? And Zutty says yes, I'll take the wheel. And Zutty started driving and all of us were asleep. And boy, we heard moo, moo and looked up and the car was in the middle of a grove of cows. Oh yes, Zutty went to sleep at the wheel. And these cows were moaning......
One cow, one we had to pay for, well its leg was broken. Because it was inbetween the bumper and the car you know.
See the cows were on the road going to pasture. And boy we were......
Was that at night or not?
Daytime, in the morning. The sun was shining and everything.
Real early in the morning.
You just sort of nodded off?
Yes. And we were just making a trip there to hear the bands and have a good time. That's all.
Well when you get to Chicago now then you got the three month lay off with the union. And we've got that about the Roulette band. Now what happens when you get with Doc Cook?

Well Doc Cook, he wanted us to join his band you know? He came out to listen to us and everything. And he liked the way I played and everything. But he wanted me to get a bass drum, an old time bass drum that was so deep you know, a twenty, say a twenty eight by sixteen or seventeen or something like that. But he liked that bass drum. And he wanted plenty of volume for that bass drum.

So I told him, I said, man, I've got a brand new set of (proto?) drums. I just had gotten them you know. And I told him that I don't think I would like to change and get a bass drum that size. So, because I figured I wasn't going to be with Charlie Cook all my life, you know. And that would have been very difficult for me to move around. That type of bass drum you know. But that's what he liked. He liked that bass drum.
Did he want it for volume. That
Oh yes. Very, very big.
Was that Harman's Dreamland.
Harman's Dreamland. It was like the Roseland is here.
Well I suppose he did have a point perhaps then?
Why sure he had a point alright. But I couldn't be stuck with a bass drum like that. See, so he and I had a falling out.
You stayed over there quite a while.
I stayed over there quite a while. Yes, because that's when Jimmy Noon and I were doubling up in the Nest. Jimmy Noon, Jerome Carrington and I were, we were doubling at the Nest at the time.
Well what time did you get to the Nest? About two in the morning or something?
No. We started at one o'clock.
Oh I see.
Started at one.
You'd play at two and then what, from eight to one or something?
Yes.
Yes. And then how long did you play at the Nest?
Man it went on and on. Sometimes we wouldn't get out of there until 10 o'clock in the morning. Ten, eleven o'clock in the morning.
Wow! What sort of a place was the Nest?

It was like, it was built from the Apex. I mean it was, the Apex was built from the Nest. See it was the Nest first, see, after hours. Strictly after hours. That's when all the gang used to come in, Bud Freeman, Eddy Condon, Benny Goodman. Of course Benny Goodman was playing with, with Ben Pollack's band out at the Pershing Hotel. See, and they would all come by.
What year would this be roughly? Do you remember?
That would have been about ......
Twenty, yes....
Because we got to Chicago in '25.
Well Jerome Carrington was a good piano player you told me?
Very,very good.
Yes, we were talking about this last time you know, but we hadn't got the machine on.

Good musician. Well he had to be to play in Charlie Cook's band. That bass drum deal, that was the thing because I would see Charlie Cook on Broadway every now and then see, and we'd talk about it you know. (LAUGHTER).
It would be funny years later.
Because he was really a doctor of music you know. Doc Cook and his Seventeen Interns, that was the name of the band.
Was he a good musician?
Yes.
He got a degree in music.
He really did?
Oh yes.
Doctor of music. Sure was so fine, so high class. Nice, you know. Just lovely.
But this (nest) was a place where a lot of society worked, you know, for them big time acts that were playing in town and all. They came there you know? And as I said before, no blacks can go
there much other than the big time pimps.
Yes, that's right. I've seen this Merryl McCormick......
Millionaires used to go there. Slumming you know?
Was it white only or not?
Not it wasn't white only but the average........
They hired a black one after hours but they had to work.
It was an expensive place?
Yes it was kind of expensive.
(unintelligible)
you know, after all these people didn't work during the day.
The guys could afford that... the pimps you know?)?
Yes.
Big time guys.

Zutty said he made seventeen dollars tips you know at the Kelly Stable. Shoot, they used to make 50, 75 dollars each a night tips. I'm telling you, Zutty used to come home with so much money. I mean, it was split down between the orchestra. I mean
between the band.
Well you mean the three of you?
Yes.
Yes, the three of us.

And Jimmy Noon was the leader but he gave them just what he took of the tips, it was split even. And Zutty would come home and just put the money down. He hadn't even counted it. Just put it down over there because he was so tired.
Yes, I bet you were.

Yes, I was a house band, yes. And Tatum, naturally he was an outstanding guy.
Well what was Slim Green he sang didn't he?
Simp Green they called him.
Simp?
Simp. Like he's simple.
Yes?
And he was in at Indianapolis.
Well what did he do?
He sang and danced and played a little triple tempo you know.
Yes. He was more of an entertainer?
Oh yes. He was really a good entertainer. And he used to sing 'Cocky, Cocky Tales for Two'.
I can remember that. He made a record of that. It was on Decca, I remember now. Yes. Well then, what were the circumstances of Roy coming in?

Well, Roy used to come in and sit in with us see. Because he was with Fletcher Henderson at the Grande Terrace at the time. So, Fletcher and the Grande Terrace had some kind of trouble and Roy quit you know. And then Roy after Sam, opened up the Three Dances again because the river had broke in and had flooded the dance floor. Yes, because it was in the basement you know, so when Sam opened again he had Roy Eldridge to come in you see with his band.
But I was still the feature you know.
And that was the band in which Roy had his brother?
That's right, yes. His brother, Scoop's Carey and Dave Young. And Truck Parham and Bumble Bee Slim, I used to call him, Johnny Collins on guitar.
(LAUGHTER?) What did you call him Bumble Bee Slim for?
Well because he reminded me of Bumble Bee Slim. I'd give guys names you know and they would stick. (LAUGHTER). Bumble Bee Slim. And we had Teddy Cole on piano. That was Cozy's brother you know.
Oh Cozy's brother?
Yes, Cozy's brother.
Eddie Cole or Teddy Cole?
No, Teddy Cole.
Teddy Cole. There was an Eddie Cole wasn't there?
Eddie Cole, he...
He's still around.
He used to be with Nobie la Sisslo (Gioserole?) a long time.
Well was he any relation of Nat Cole?
Yes, why sure.
Eddie Cole was his brother?
Why sure, that's right.
Well that was a good little band.
Oh it was. It was a real lovely, lovely band. And Joe was making all the arrangements for us you know.
Haven't you heard any of their records? ( ?). That was a terrific record.
Yes. That was the same personnel that you were working?
That's right.
Yes, well I've just forgotten the personnel. I knew Joe was on it, but I wasn't sure of the others.
Because it wasn't just one trumpet, it was like a little organ for Roy you know. Of course he didn't like the records for a while, but now he's beginning to like them you know.
He didn't like them?
No. At first he didn't care much for them.
Oh, I've always heard people talk about Hecklers' Hop and whatever was on the back
of that and as almost his best, favorite record.
Well yes. And then after that we recorded for Mildred Bailey too. Did you get those records?
Yes, I think I've got all of them. And how long did this gig run at the Three Deuces?
Oh that ran quite over a year. And then Roy was taken sick. That's how that little band broke up. Roy taken sick.
What was the matter with him?

Oh just fatigue. Nothing really serious you know. And that's when Tatum got the band. And Tatum had a drummer friend in Chicago by the name of Winston. And he wanted this guy to play the drums with him. See, and that's when Marge and I came to New York.
I had a brand new Ford you know, and we were just taking our time and come on....
How long would it take you to drive to New York in those days?
Oh well we stopped so much. You know, we'd take our time. We didn't have to rush about anything. Because I didn't have no job.
Oh, I see.
We were just coming to New York.
Right, right.

And we went up to see old Brud (Breaud). And then old woman Brud found us a place to stay. Right in the place I was telling you about the 'House of Meditation'. Like with Miss Cotton. Yes, old Brud (Breaud) fixed us up. Because I did but have fifty cents when I came out of the Harlem Tunnel.
Really?
That's all I had. Shot right on up to Brud's (Breaud St). And Brud (Breaud) straightened us out right away.
He was a good guy.
Yes, he was.

And we were hungry because we'd eaten, had a bag of salted peanuts and we ate that I think all the way from Philadelphia to New York or Pittsburg. We went to Pittsburg, that was our last stop, looking for Charlie. Didn't find, couldn't find him. My brother.
And we ate these salted peanuts. So hungry. And fifty cents when we came out of that tunnel. But we weren't unhappy. We were just as happy as lobsters (dogs).
Just like we were coming here and Zutty had a job. Because Zutty said we'll go right to Brand and I'll borrow some money from him. He'll give us a place to stay. We'll stay with him.
He used a different name for Brand. What did he call him? His name was Wallman
Wallman Brand
I thought he used a, oh perhaps he said Brody

And he had a beautiful apartment up on St. Nicholas Avenue. We went directly to his apartment but he didn't have an extra bedroom. He didn't have room for us. Meanwhile, it was kind of late at night and he cooked dinner for us. It was on Sunday. I'll never forget, it was on a Sunday and they didn't have much left for dinner. But he cooked some other things for us and gave us a big dinner at that time of the night.
Then he said, he didn't have a room for us but he took us down to Miss Cotton's where the 'House of Meditation' was and had her to give us a room. And he gave Zutty some money.
Oh that was a good friend.

I'm telling you. He really looked out for us. But we were as happy as, we weren't worried at all. We were just as happy as we could be. We were in New York, we made it. And we were happy. And the next day Zutty contacted (Mezz?) and let him know we were in town. And (Mezz?) was right up there. And on the Monday night (Mezz?) took us down to the (Hickory) House for sizzling steaks because Joe Marsala was in there. Everyone was so glad to see Zutty and me you know, and Joe Marsala we had dinner in there. Oh, had a delicious dinner and Joe Marsala, he gave Zutty some money and told Zutty he wanted him to play the jam session on Sunday afternoon. And that was Zutty's first gig in New York was the next week on a Sunday afternoon, they had jam sessions. He wanted Zutty to come and sit in and play. And he paid Zutty thirty-five dollars which was a lot of money for us.
Yes, at that time.
And Mezzrow was right with us from beginning to end. He really was with us.
That's when Mezz, mae had quit Mezz see and he was so disgusted and things like that. He said, I think I'll commit suicide. I
said, well man, if you commit suicide I said, leave the car for me.

Because meanwhile we were out, I think it was the first week or second week we were here, Zuddy hadn't made the payment on the car. And he had let them know he was coming to New York. Well they contacted him here you know from the automobile place and Zuddy told them they'd just have to take it because he wasn't working.

And he didn't have any trouble with them. They understood it because he had reported to the Company... He had almost paid for the car but he didn't have any money and Mezz didn't have any money. And we couldn't ask [unintelligible 4)] still about seven hundred dollars. And still it was a brand new '36 Ford and fancy. All chrome all the way around. Oh yes, and so we used Mezz's car because Mezz had a car. And that's when Zuddy ......
Joe Marsala was the cause of me getting my first payment on the car. It was $27.50 a month.
Yes, that's right.
See, and so Joe had me to come down .....
I told him that. That Sunday, you know, the very first week we were in town.
I remember the very first time I came to New York they were having those in there, the Hickory House on Sunday.
Yes.
Jazz session. And Lion was there.
Hot Lips Page. We worked there together.
Yes, that's right. Yes, that must have been about '37 because ....
It was. '37 or '38.
Oh '38. '37 I came and Hot Lips was, everywhere I went I ran into Hot Lips. Well then what did you do then after this. I mean what, where did you begin to work?
Well that's when I went into with Fats Waller or something like that? Did I go into Cannie's Inn with Fats Waller?
Well let's see. This guy says ....
You went to Nicks.
Oh I went to Nicks.
You went to Nicks.
Yes, Mezzrow's Disciples of Swing in November '37.
Oh yes.
It was in '37 when we came because the car wasn't two years old.
Yes, he says, you were at the Three Deuces and remained, became a member of Roy Eldridges band in September '36. Left the following year to return to New York.
That's right.
Yes. And featured at Nicks in early '38.
Yes, with Bobby Hackett and Eddie Candor (Commin?) got me that job. Because Nicks didn't just wanted me on the stand. I had my drums on the floor, see, and ....
An added attraction.
Yes, an added attraction, see. So old Bobby Hackett would putting me on on each set you know.
And it says here, with Bechet too.
Well he told you about Bechet
That was a little later, yes.
Yes, he came in later.
Yes. That's when Zutty had got his own band in Nicks. But he had, he left Nicks and went back there didn't you?
Yes, I went from here, I sure did.
See in '39 and '40 made own trio and sextet at Nicks. Also led at Village Vanguard and Kelley's. But you said you weren't at Kelley's. No that's wrong.
He went to the Vanguarde from Nicks. That's after Nick fired Zutty.
Before taking up long residency at Ryan's from March '41 until '43. Were you leading your own group in Ryan's?
Took the first band in there.
Oh you did? Who did you have in there?
I had Sidney DeParis.
Joe Eldridge.
Joe, no at the Vanguarde you mean?
No, Ryan's.
No at Ryan's.
Oh, Ryan's. I had Sidney DeParis, Joe Eldridge and Don Frye.
Al Hall?
Al Hall. And then from there then Tibbs taken over. LeRoy Tibbs?
Yes?
We used to play with LeRoy Smith's band. And he came in after Don at the (Down?).
Yes. What sort of a piano player was he?
Very good.
I never heard him.

He's a show man you know. He played all those fine Gershwin things. Because that's what Ally Ross used to do too see. Play all, all Rogers and Hart and all those kind of things. He was that kind of fine piano player.
Well that, well that period in New York then is all small bands?
Yes.
Yes.
That was small bands.
And then you moved to L.A. With a quartet at Billy Berg's in 1943?
That's right. That's right.
What made you go out there? (Marty Goub)
Well, Mike (sure?), he wanted me to come out to Billy Berg's you know and play.
He went out there to California to make the picture.
Picture, Stormy Weather.

Stormy Weather. And then he called me from California and said he wanted to live out there. And I didn't because I was working at McCoy's. And I had a good job and we had a beautiful little apartment. Small but beautifully furnished and Zutty called me and said he loved California and we were going to move out there.

I said, we'll talk about it when you come home, before I'll leave New York. He came back and he told me, said, and he went back to Ryan's and they had advertised Zutty was coming back that he had finished his picture work. He'd made this picture out there. What was the picture?
'Stormy Weather'.
'Stormy Weather'. And I told
Zutty we're not going to California. So two days after he had come back and they advertised he was coming back in Ryan's sent him a telegram and told him he had him set in Billy Berg's.
For my quartet.
For his quartet. And Mike did all of the booking and everything. And Zutty said, well, we're going.
And the quartet consisted of Joe Eldridge, Kenny Watts, Bass Hill and myself.
I think Kenny Watts was on the piano.
Yes.
Zutty had taken him to California with him.
You and Joe Eldridge evidently were pretty close?
Oh yes.
Zutty loved Joe Eldridge, Zutty did everything possible for Joe Eldridge.
Was Joe like Roy or different?
Yes, he was a little different. I think there was a little jealousy there somewhere, you know.
Because Roy didn't give him work.
Yes. Roy had a chance to help him a lot and he didn't.
Roy didn't give him work; Roy didn't help him. He had a wife and two children and we tried to get her to move to California, tried to get his wife because Joe was doing so well.

Benny Carter had give him a good job copying, you know. And Joe had beautiful writing. And Benny Carter had him all set to stay right in California because he had this good job for him. And Joe was really doing good.

Because Zutty had said we were coming back to New York after he finished his engagement at Billy Berg's because he picked up the option and he stayed longer than you'd intended to stay in there. And I cried because I didn't like California.
Now why didn't you like it?

Because Zutty told me on the 'phone and when he got back that the sun shined every day and it was so beautiful. And when we got out there the sun didn't shine for three months. And I said, where is the sunshine? I didn't like it, my dog didn't like it bringing down and we hated it.

We'd sit by ourselves both of us and cried every day, wanted to come back to New York. We were living with Jimmy Mundy and his wife and they had two great big Chow dogs and I was afraid they were going to kill Barney. Before we'd go out or something they say they'd put their dogs out in the yard and bring Barney in the house.

But any time we'd be out I'd was worried to death that those dogs were going to get in the house. Because they hated Barney, another dog you know. And we had a chance to get a little apartment, it was during the war and there was a couple who lived around the corner from the Mundy's who had a nice little house. It was a duplex, two family and her husband had been drafted and she joined the WACS. And she was lonesome without him and she wanted in the WACS.

And the only way we could get the house right away was to let her stay in the house until the WACS called her you know, called for her to go into the WACS. And so, and if she was in there or not I wanted to get out of there with my dog. Because we went to d Paul Whiteman broadcast one evening because Jimmy was arranging for Paul Whiteman. And we came back home and

my dog was almost dead.
Jimmy had come home and let the dogs in and
they had almost killed my dog.
Your dog was a she wasn't she?
No.
It was a he dog?
And he didn't know how to fight because he had been raised in New York and you know he was on a leash all the time.
Yes, yes.

And we came home and my dog was almost dead. And I went around the corner and told the woman, the only way you could get the house was to buy her furnishings. And I told her I would buy her furnishings and we were ready to move in that day. And we moved in. And the woman stayed with us for about three months but she was nice. Very nice a lovely person. And Dorothy Mundy told me I wouldn't like living with a stranger. I told her I can live with anybody. I get along with anybody. And found out the woman was a lovely woman and (Barney?) and I had a place for ourselves. And the people living on the other side were so nice.
They were a Jewish couple and we became fast

friends. And so when it was time, when Zutty's, Zutty could have left Billy Berg's he said we'll go back to New York. I said, no, I like California (LAUGHTER). And then I became very close with Alan Dooley Wilson and his wife. He lived across the street.
Oh really?
Oh yes. They adopted me. I was their daughter.
How long did this job at Berg's last then?
About a year. Yes, they just kept picking up his option.

It's strange isn't it how the business sort of altered in that way. I mean you used to go in a place and stay a year. I mean that doesn't happen any more. Because that was one thing I remember Coleman Hawkins said to me not so long before he died, he said, you know the trouble is that in the old days people knew you in a certain place. And when they came into the city they'd come by. But nowadays they don't know who's going to be there when they come in.
I think there are advantages to those long runs.
Well look how long Wilbur DeParis stayed in Jimmy Ryans.
Right.
And Zutty could have stayed in Jimmy Ryan's as long as he wanted to stay. Because they always, Zutty opened the store. The very first band that went in Jimmy Ryan's.
They'd say that all the time.
Zutty got the store started.
And another thing that Max Gordon at the Vanguard. Zutty changed his clientele altogether until he had such fancy trade until Zutty told him to put some table clothes on. Because it was a joint.
No table cloths, and Zutty said to him you have to put some table cloths on, fix the place up. All these fine people coming in you know.
It was the calypso band wds drawing them in. Gerald Clark and his calypso band.
Oh that was alternating with you?
That was alternating and then .....
Well who did you have down there?
I had Joe Eldridge. And first I had Albert Nicholas. Albert Nicholas and...
Eddie Heywood.
Eddie Heywood. See, that's
how I opened up. And then later Edridge came in and Clyde Hart came in. And then Don Frye came in. And that's the outfit we brought over to Jimmy Ryans.
I see, yes.
Because (Milt Gabler (Lou Dagen)) was having those sessions every Sunday. See and Jimmy got the idea that he wanted to have me to come in for regular you know.
Yes.
That's why I always say that whole people forget. Zuttie has given a lot of musicians who have big names, he's given them a break.
Well one thing I was, I was thinking about on the way home last week after we did it. You know I don't think I ever heard, you know you worked, you had Bubber Miley in your band like that.
Yes.
Well, what sort of a guy was Bubber?
The sweetest guy in the world.
Yes?
Yes. He used to come to our house for dinner and things. And I knew his sisters too. Because when Bubber was taken sick his sister came around to the M & S Theater to see if she could
get a little something you know from old Sterling. Sterling you know, he was the manager of the theater.
Did you say M & S Theater?
M & S.
Yes, M & S.
Where was that?
That was 135th Street near the Apollo.
Oh, I didn't know that.
Near the Apollo. I think it's a picture house now. I think so. And we had a pretty good band. Ralph Cooper was the leader of the band.
That was a big band.
Yes, that was a big band.
Well I mean, I always wondered what, why Bubber never went back with Duke? You know, nobdoy's ever said anything, but there must have been a little falling out there I think.

There must have been something. Because we had heard their first broadcast in Chicago when Duke made that coast to coast hook up like you know. And Bubber Miley was in the band at that time because we all went to Carroll Dickerson's house, our

whole band. Louis Armstrong and our whole band. We went over to Carroll Cat Dickerson's house to hear this broadcast. It was coming in in the afternoon like. It was sort of like a special deal. And old Bubber Miley played East St. Louis Teedle-oo Blues. Boy, he sure did growl and go on and on.
Well he was really the strongest thing in the band to begin with wasn't he?
Yes he was. He and Tricky Sam.
Yes, but I mean he was before Tricky.
Oh sure. Sure.
As I remember, I don't know, it could have been a drinking problem with Duke. Bubber was a drinker.
Oh he was?
Yes. And that's what could have happened. It couldn't have been his disposition. He was always smiling and was so sweet and everything. But maybe, I wouldn't say....
No.
But it could probably be the
drinking problem because he drank himself to death, Bubber did. He really did.
Well of course the other thing is too that (Artie Whetsol) was a Washington friend of Duke's too.
Yes.

So that may, you know, there may have been a problem there with two trumpets and if Bubber took off once, it was difficult to bring him back until they got the bigger band. But it always seemed a pity that he didn't stay there.

But in the last band I was always with Zutty. That's why I know what happened got to go with him every place and they made Ralph Cooper the leader of the band and I don't know what big gig you all were going on because you had these beautiful new uniforms and it was night you were rehearsing.

And Ralph Cooper was supposed to play the saxophone. He didn't know how to hold a saxophone. They were teaching him that night and I saw it, I was there. They had to teach him how to hold the saxophone.
Well what was.....
They were making pictures that
night of the band.
I think I know he was an MC, but what else did he do? Was he a dancer or something?
He had been a dancer at one time.
So had Cooper.
Yes. Had these beautiful new uniforms and they were making pictures that night of the band because the band was going to do some big gig. And Louis Metcalf was in that band.
No, I think it was Huck and...
Was that the guy that told me that his wife had better not tell him when he's wrong?
Yes, Henry Goodwin.
Henry Goodwin.
Henry Goodwin and Gus Clung McLeod.
That's who it was.
That was our trumpets.
And it was a big band and a beautiful band. But what killed me was the leader didn't know how to hold a saxophone. They had to keep on correcting him you know and he had his hands on the keys ......
One time he had them upside down. (LAUGHTER).
That was a scene. Oh my land...
That was a good looking band.
Yes. And those uniforms. I shall never forget the color, it was blue. A pale blue.
Blue and white pants.
White pants.
And double breasted ....
Oh they were beautiful. Beautiful.
Well how long did that M & S Theater run then?
Well it didn't last too long.
Ah, that's why. I never heard of it.
It didn't last too long.
It was in opposition kind of to the Apollo.
And there was the Harlem with the La Fayette and the Apollo?
The Apollo Opera House, that was it.
That was it?
Yes.
That was it. Changed it to
I'll change it to M & S.
I wonder why I hadn't heard of that.
Yes change it from the M and S to the Harlem.
To the Harlem.
To the Harlem, yes.
Oh, oh, that's interesting. Well we better go back to California though. Now he says after Billy Berg's you played with Paul Howard's band and T-Bone Walker?
Oh yes, yes. Yes after Billy Berg's. Then I played at Streets of Paris and then we played at the Swanee Inn with Shelton Brooks, Junior, and I and Rose Murphy the Chi Chi. She was there.
How big a band was Paul Howard's? At that time?
Paul Howard.
Yes, they say you worked with him.
Yes, it must have been just one or two nights.
You see that's what, you see they've got this information out of magazines and they see, they might see you, it might have been just two or three days.
Yes, that's right, yes.
What about T-Bone Walker?
T-Bone Walker, that was really a nice job.
Oh yes?
Because the night we opened up Dinah Washington was going to join ...
Lionel?
Lionel. The night we opened up because that was her big party, giving her a big send off.
It was way out in California.
Yes, it was way out past Watts, yes. And we had Carl Jefferson on the tenor sax and Norman Bowden on trumpet and Mingus on bass.
Charlie Mingus?
And little Shorty, a little short trombone player and Garland Finney on piano. And the band, they loved everything Duke played, see.
This is, whose band?
This is T-Bone Walker's band.
Oh, T-Bone Walker's band?
Yes.
Yes?
The loved everything, boy, we used to really play all those Duke Ellington tunes. And everybody had a real feeling for them you know. That went on about, about a year.
Yes.
Well T-Bone, I mean he wasn't just singing blues then? I mean it was....
Yes, he was singing the blues.
And playing his guitar.
Well I mean he played in the band when you were doing these Ellington things too?
Yes.
Well T-Bone was a pretty good musician?
Boggano right.
He was a nice guy.
And how they used to line up and give that guy the money. Boy they used to just get in line to give this guy money.
Which joint was this, which club was this you were playing in?
This was the Brown Sister.
The Brown Sisters?

Yes, they were great gamblers. They used to gamble with the Chinese people out there. See, and boy when you come into the place they had a big chef that was frying chicken and hot biscuits. Boy and I had taken old Teagarden out there one night and that cat ate three orders of fried chicken and biscuits. Hot dog. And you could see, that's the first thing you saw when you walked in the place. Was this big chef and so clean and nice you know. And that fried chicken, you could smell that fried chicken. And boy, that was too much. We used to just really......

And that's why I say that Zutty had such a good heart. He never thought about black or white. Dave came to California from the Navy. Checked into a hotel, oh, like the Hilton, a good hotel. And he looked in the 'phone book or in the musician book and found our telephone number. And he called Zutty and he told him he was at this hotel. And so he asked Zutty if we were rooming or if we had a house, an apartment. And Zutty told him, he said I have a house. He said, I'll be right over, I'm checking out. And he came over with his bag on his back and
he stayed with us for about two weeks before he came to New York. He stayed right with us and he slept up in our living room on the....
He left us to go live with Rudy Vallee.
Yes, he left us, he stayed with us for about two weeks and Zutty took him out to the his gig. Took him out to his job.

Because a lot of the gals, the waitresses they worked in different record shops you know. They knew just who he was, see. And I told him, I said, now listen I'm going to take you out tonight, I said, but if you get drunk I'm going to call the SPs on you. He said, you know something, I believe you would do that. I said, you damn right I would.

And when he said he was coming over to live with us, Zutty said, fine, come on we'll put you on the couch in the front. And I said, well let me hid my whiskey. I hid my whiskey because I said, I don't want him getting drunk in here. I said, because he's noted for getting drunk. A sweet guy, I loved him. And boy he came over and took all his things out of his bag and he was at home right in

our house.
So I told him, I said, now I don't want you getting drunk Dave, messing up my house. 'I want, no I wont, I wont. And one night ....
You had hit the whiskey.

I had hid the whiskey, but I went with Zutty to work and Dave hadn't come home for dinner or anything. And so when we came back he had gotten in, we gave him a key. And he had gotten drunk and vomited in the bathroom. And I said, now listen, and he found the whiskey. Well I put it in the cooler, what they call a cooler, way in the back, thought he'd never find it, but he found it. And I said, I don't clean up after Zutty, Dave. Because Zutty doesn't do this. And I'm not going to clean up after you. You're welcome to stay here, but if you do it one more time you're not going to stay here. And I mean it.

So he straightened up and then one day we kept worrying, he hadn't come home. He didn't come home before Zutty went to work and he didn't come home that night. And the next day he didn't come home. And so Zutty said, I wonder what's happened to Dave? And Zutty went out looking for him on Vine Street and all.
Here, Rudy Vallee had picked him up and taken
him out to his house.
Out to his house.
And he stayed out there for about a week.
Instead of our house guest, he was Rudy Vallee's.
Rudy Vallee's. And Rudy Vallee picked him up and took him home.
He gave Marge a nice little jacket.
It was a, you know, a (field?) jacket like. It just fit me because he was so small.
I still have his practice pad.
Have you really?
Yes. He gave me his pad.
Well I always read that he was the best white drummer of them all.
He was boy.
In my opinion. I guess it's a matter of what style you like, but I think he was....
And a sweet guy. Oh we loved him so much. Just like our own.
Well now, after T-Bone, it says you do Orson Welles radio show, worked with Teddy Bunn
and then Slim Galliard in the Spring of '45.
Yes, that was at Billy Berg's new place. They had moved on Vine Street about this time.
Did you, do you ever hear anything of Teddy Bunn?
Teddy Bunn no.
He's still out there.
He's still out there?
The last time we heard he was here you know with Louis Jordan's band.
Oh was he?
Yes. They played the Metropole.
Oh, that was how long ago?
Oh Lord. That must have been about, I guess about ten years ago.
He lived in Riverside didn't he?
Yes, he lived in Riverside and then he moved to Sacramento. Yes, and he's living in there for a while. But in the meantime, before this happened you know, Nappy Lamdre was making up his band.
Yes?
So I went on the road with Edmure Lew, Nappy Lemon, Brad Gowan and Stew Fletcher.
Oh?
And Pud Brown.
Yes?
Yes. We made a tour of all the colleges. We played most all the colleges. Out on the West Coast.
On the West Coast.
Oh?
From one end to the other.
Yes. You all were gone about, just about six weeks I think.
Yes, about that.
Yes, six weeks.
Yes, Stew Fletcher, he was with Norvo at one time wasn't he? You say he's out on the West Coast too?
Yes. He lives out there. He and his wife, Arlene. And his son was over to see us not so long ago. Well about, before I was taken sick.
Oh yes, yes.
Yes.
Because Zutt y did so much recording while he was in California. He was really quite a lot of making nice money because he was doing a lot of bread recording.
Dave Dexter had me all set.
(And Capitol you know?) for
And then every once in a while, a little movie deals while.
Sugar Charles Robinson, I played for him, yes recorded with him.
Yes, well that of course is, if you can fall into that picture that where you can, you could make a lot of money?
Yes. And then those moving picture deals coming in every once in a while and all.
Well the Slim Gaillard deal was also purely, it was also very popular wasn't it?

Oh, Lord yes. And that was some rhythm we had going. He and Tiny Brown, the bass player, Slim Gaillard and myself. Boy and we'd get gigs to play down at the May Company during lunch hour and all that kind of stuff, you know.
And that place, they was had Harry the Hipster in there.
Oh yes.
Harry the Hipster.
And that place was so crowded that he'd have the ropes up at 8.30 at night, you couldn't get in there. All movie stars.
Big time movie stars.
Oh, he was doing some business. Believe me.
And if old Slim Guilard would know a movie star and what picture he had been in, well he'd act the picture right on the stand you know.
(LAUGHTER).
Avocado Seed Soup and all that. Hippopotamus Chittlings and all that kind of stuff.
(LAUGHTER).
He really had a funny .....
And they went on a tour. You know, came East on a tour. Because that was in '46 when I came out and joined you in Chicago.
That's right. And we went to Washington DC.
Boston.
Boston.
Theatres.
Just the trio?
Yes, the trio.
In theaters you know.
Yes?
Yes. You really had a varied career.

And boy, old Tiny Brown put all of his underwear in a tub. He figured he was going to wash them out and everything. And I'd look at him in front playing that bass boy and there that cat didn't have no drawers on. (LAUGHTER).
You knew that?
Yes, I knew that he had put them all in this tub see. And he was going to wash them out and dry them out, but he'd get going.

But Zutty had, he went on that tour with them through the William Morris office. He had them to take care of the business. Because Slim Gaillard was known to be a character that would take your money. And he was so surprised the first week they got paid, they paid Zutty directly from the box office, from the management of a theater.
Oh?
Oh yes, because that's the
only way Zutt y told them..... Jimmy Rushing did that for me too.
Yes.
Because in Washington DC at the Howard Theater, Lucky Millinder saw that I got my money.
Yes. It was still the William Morris office that your business was really taken care of. Because you were still, you were still with them.
Oh sure.
And that's the only way Zutt y would do it because Slim was known to be a character you know.
Well, ...
I remember once on the trip when we went to get on the train he was going to make Zutt y pay for all the fares for all the boys. (LAUGHTER). Because he had, said he had lost his money.
Yes, he had a doctor with him. Some doctor was supposed to be giving him some kind of shots. But I believe it was nothing but water. Because this doctor was a quack.

And he had his wife and she was a character also. And they left a beautiful home in California. Talk about a beautiful place. They had servants. Because they had a maid, why when you'd go there, why the maid would open the door. They both went out on the road and they didn't pay the taxes the whole time they were out. They didn't pay, they didn't pay anything. They went back and their home was sold at auction. That's the kind of guy he was.

Well this thing where you've got here Zutty. Galliard Slim '46. Wingy Manone (Wingy Lemone?) '47. Eddie Condon '48. Joe Marsala '48, Nappy Lamare '49. Were these sort of mostly things you were working out of California?
No. Condon (Norman?) was out on the road. He was with Wingy (Wingy?) in California.
Yes, I was with Wingy Manone (Wingy?) (Lemone?) out in California. But I joined Condon in Chicago.
Ah!
See, because Condon had Bud Freeman, Peanuts Hucko and Dick Cary on piano and Dave Manning on bass.
Who was the trumpet player?
The trumpet player?
Yes.
Ah...
Wild Bill or Jimmy ....
Bobby Hackett
Oh, Bobby Hackett.
Bobby Hackett, yes. Bobby Hackett and a fine trombone player was out of Fred Waring's band, he was on the trombone. And that's when we played at, that place on Randolph Street?
Ah, the Blue Note?
The Blue Note.
Oh yes. So when you, you've got Nappy Lamore '49, did you go back to California?
Oh yes.
Oh I see.
(Unintelligible) that band.
Yes, California was really your home at this point?
Oh yes.
Yes.
That was our headquarters.
Yes. I see.

And Zutty went back and you had worked for Nappy Lumare (Lemone?) in Studio City Club in '47. Because I never forget, I still have it on the postcard. When Zutty got through with this road tour with Hacket and Condon and was coming back to California, they sent out postcards. Zutty's back and we got him (LAUGHTER). We mailed that to the mailing list. Zutty went right back in Club 47.
And then after I left Club 47 I went to the Knotty Pine.
Knotty Pine? (LAUGHTER).
The Knotty Pine. It was a cowboy joint. They had Spade Cooley and all that gang. And jockeys because they had a training track near the Knotty Pine. It was at Victory and something way out there.
With Bernie Billings.
Yes, with Bernie Billings and Bobby Troup?
Yes, Bobby Troup.
Oh, (he came to appear there?)?
Yes.
Yes?
Well Bobby Tru was a big man. He was in ....
Was he?
He made a tour of London you know.
Oh yes. But does he do much himself now?
I don't think he plays so much.
No, I didn't think he did.
He writes and he arranges a lot too. I see his name sometimes.
Well then I've got here, (Art Hodes in Chicago 1950, Bobby Hackett '51. And that's before joining Bernie Billings in Los Angeles, is that right?
Oh yes.
Yes.
No, no. That was afterwards. Because in '51 we were in Europe.
We were leaving for Europe.
Yes. Well the way he's got it Art Hodes, Chicago '50, Bobby Hackett Spring '51, Bernie Billings, Los Angeles, August '51, sailed to Europe in November '51.
That's right.
That's right? And then you tour with Mezz?
Yes. Joined Mezz over there.
And Hot Lips?
Yes, Mezz, Lips and I we didn't play with Mezz.
Oh?
We played in ( Casino la Zue ?).
In Belgium.
Belgium, yes.
Well was that a festival or was that ....
No, that was a steady job.
It was a gambling casino.
How long did you play there?
Three months.
Yes.
Oh.
The whole season.
Yes.
And then we went back again for something.
Well the next time we went for a festival or something.
Yes, we went for some festival or something.
See this was a big place and Zuddy and them played in a room they called the New Orleans Room.
Oh.
They had seven different rooms.

And then they didn't allow the musicians to gamble in there at all. And then they had a concert room where Hazel Scott, Maurice Chevalier and all, they appeared there at the same time, in the concert room.
Yma Sumac played there.
Oh, that was..... Well did that place keep going like this with sort of big names or did it change the policy?
All the big names ....
I think it's still .......
I suppose so, yes.
It was a big gambling casino.
You couldn't go into the gambling room, you weren't allowed in there at all.
And all you saw parked around there were Cadillacs. American cars.
Because they had a concert room. And then they had a big movie theater and then they had this New Orleans Room and then an Argentine Room.
Extraordinary!
And they never played nothing but Argentine music.
Tangos.
Tangos and things.
A beautiful place. And the New Orleans Room......
Fresh flowers every day.
They had it fixed sort of like New Orleans and when you walked in they had big white horses on each side you know. Oh it was a ....... But no gambling. You could not gamble in there.
Well then he says you went with after that you went with Bill Coleman, toured with Bill Coleman?
Yes, that's right. While I was over there with Mezz.
Yes?
But Zutt y got fed up with it and he didn't want to stay for Bill Coleman. He wanted to come home. But Bill Coleman said he could make so much money.
That was when Dickie Wells was with you wasn't it?
Yes.
And it was very cold and everything.

And Zutt y was tired. But I begged, I was the cause of Zutt y staying there. I said, and Bill Coleman and Lil, his wife, they came to the hotel and they just begged Zutt y to stay so they could make some money. Said, man, they'd made so much money on Zutt y's name, Zutt y's work. And so I told Zutt y, I said, let's stay. I said, after all, let's help them too. You helped Mezz.
Yes?

And that's the only reason Zutt y stayed, because Zutt y said he was ready to come home. He was sick of Europe. He was just sick of it. And so through me he made the tour because he was fed up and ready to come home.
Well I do think one thing about it that you'd find the winters kind of hard over there.
But we become accustomed to it. I was glad we stayed in Switzerland so long and you know a few of those cold countries. When I came back here the cold weather didn't bother me.
Well I know, but I didn't really mean the temperature so much, but the fact that the houses are not you know, warm like you're accustomed to here.

Well our hotels, Zutty told you, we stayed in the best hotels and we were always, we were always comfortable. We stayed where they had hot water. They told Zutty you know, our hotel even in Paris was a second class hotel, but it was the Hotel (Renzerez ?). And we had hot water twenty four hours a day which was unusual for the type of hotel it was. It was a very old hotel, but a very fine hotel, well kept.
Which hotel was that Marge?
Hotel (Renzerez?).
(Renzerez?).
East Boulevard, and (Oman?). Montmartre
East Boulevard, and (Oman?). Montmartre
I don't know that one.
It's over the museum by.
How did you get on speaking French, did you learn to speak it well?
Well pretty good.
Did your New Orleans background help there a bit?
Yes, it helped a lot.

And when Zutty would speak French, yes when he spoke French they really said he spoke like a Frenchman. I was kind of learning, they would laugh at me. I mispronounced so many things. But when Zutty would speak they would say, ah oui! You know, because, and then I wanted to go to Berlitz school. I was getting pretty good in the meantime to speak French. And Zutty said, there's no use going through all that. So I learned mine from the House of Balenciaga (Rue de ?). Who was really crazy about me. And I met her in the Columbia She came up and taught me how to count in French. And I loved learned that.
In one night.
To handle that money.
(unintelligible) for Marge.

Yes. And then we'd go in stores and Zutty would say to me, what did they say Marge? I said, I don't know. And he said, let's get the hell out of here. And they'd bring somebody in that spoke English you know. Because we were going to spend some money.

Well then, this tape is going to run out in a minute. But after Europe you've come back to New York and then you work around, it says, Stuyvesant, Casino, Central Plaza, Metropole and then a long time at Ryans etc. And that brings us more or less through doesn't it?
Yes. Because at Ryan's when I came back I started working in Ryan's with Wilbur DeParis.
Wilbur DeParis.
Yes, yes. And then you carry on though with, yes and then with Tony Parenti (Carandi?).
Yes. (Carandi?).
Max Kaminsky, yes. The films, let's see, he says, 'Stormy Weather' '43. 'New Orleans', '46. That was the film you were in with Lee and Billy Holiday
wasn't it? New Orleans? Yes, yes.
Yes. And what about 'Turned Up Toes' in '49, what was that? A movies called Turned Up Toes. Do you remember that?
No I don't. 'Turned Up Toes' Galliard Another picture I made was the one with the Slim Gaylord Vallee trio with Rudy Vallee and Pat O'Brian was in that picture.
Well what about the picture with Cesar Romero?
Oh yes.
Which one then Marge?
Cesar Romero.
Oh!
And Paul Douglas.
Well do you think that was called Toes' Turned Up Xxxx?
Maybe that was Turned Up Toes?
Maybe that was.
Because Zutty worked in them, he didn't know what they were called. And then now about Danny Kaye's picture.
Yes.
Which was that?
'A Song is Born.'
'A Song is Born.'
Oh, you were in that too?
Yes.
Oh yes, yes.
Yes, yes. Oh this was all the time you were out there?
Yes.
Well of course that also made sense of staying out there didn't it? Records, and...
Yes. And when we left Europe everybody was saying that Zuttie could come to work out there. He could go right back in Club 47.
Well when did you sell the house out there then?
When we left for Europe.
Oh I see.
We didn't own the house.
We didn't own the house.
It was our furniture. But they wrote to us in Europe. I liked the house so much I wanted to buy it, but the woman wouldn't sell, Mrs. (KAPLAN ?). But while we were in Europe they
contacted us through our band, the Bank of America that Mrs. (KAPLAN ?) had passed away and her daughter who had charge of the estate, contacted us in Europe to buy the house.
And you would have done I suppose .......................

segments.chapter: Boyhood in New Orleans
segments.title: Tape 1 opening and Zutty's birthplace, Bunkie, Louisiana
segments.summary: Dance restarts the tape after a distorted take; Zutty says he was born in Bunkie, Louisiana, and the date is garbled.

segments.chapter: Boyhood in New Orleans
segments.title: Aunt Carrie, first drums and the second line bands
segments.summary: His Aunt Carrie, a teacher and pianist, and his mother encouraged him; she bought his first drums. He beat on chairs, followed New Orleans second-line bands and moved there at about ten.

segments.chapter: Boyhood in New Orleans
segments.title: Cousin Willie Bontemps passed off as his uncle
segments.summary: Marge prompts the story of his cousin Willie Bontemps, Aunt Carrie's son, called his uncle because married women could not teach school. Willie played bass, guitar and banjo and took Zutty to rehearsals.

segments.chapter: Boyhood in New Orleans
segments.title: Jack Carey's band and his Tiger Rag
segments.summary: Willie played in Jack Carey's jazz and marching band; Jack, Mutt Carey's brother, played trombone and was famous for Tiger Rag. Dance dates this to about 1913.

segments.chapter: Boyhood in New Orleans
segments.title: Viney Monroe, who helped raise him
segments.summary: Zutty explains that Viney Monroe worked for his mother in Bunkie and helped bring him up and take him around, though she was not a musician.

segments.chapter: Boyhood in New Orleans
segments.title: His father leaves; hunting and the rabbit story
segments.summary: His father had left before the move to New Orleans; Zutty remembers him hunting and bringing home rabbits, and why his mother never liked rabbit.

segments.chapter: Boyhood in New Orleans
segments.title: Big Eye Louis's band at Palms Road House and its cooking
segments.summary: Playing with Big Eye Louis at the Palms Road House, band members cooked and hunted; Big Eye fried rabbit with garlic, and Maurice Durand and Walter Decou were hunters too.

segments.chapter: Boyhood in New Orleans
segments.title: Steve Lewis, his first drum teacher, and the Piron band
segments.summary: Steve Lewis, a pianist who could not read but played with A.J. Piron, encouraged Zutty. Zutty names the good musicians in Piron's band, including Pete Bocage.

segments.chapter: Boyhood in New Orleans
segments.title: Papa Tio and the origin of Mood Indigo
segments.summary: Zutty and Marge say Tio taught many clarinetists and that Mood Indigo came from him through Barney Bigard to Duke Ellington. They puzzle over the credits on records, including Mills.

segments.chapter: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
segments.title: First job at the Rose Bud movie theater
segments.summary: Zutty explains that the Rose Bud was a neighborhood movie house, distinct from the downtown Lyric, where he and Steve Lewis got his first job playing for the pictures. Marge raises the Louis hiring story, which Dance defers.

segments.chapter: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
segments.title: Accompanying silent films and the effects equipment
segments.summary: Playing for pictures was good training in timing. Zutty and Marge describe the effects he had to make, such as crashes, whistles and the steamboat whistle.

segments.chapter: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
segments.title: Sleigh bells bought at Connie's Inn in 1929
segments.summary: The sleigh bells in the case were bought in 1929 for a Christmas show at Connie's Inn, when Hal Baquet played Santa Claus. Dance remarks on percussion fashions today.

segments.chapter: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
segments.title: Stop Thief pistol shots and the slapstick
segments.summary: On Fate Marable's boat Zutty fired blank shells hit with a mallet for the tune Stop Thief, and he used a slapstick on Ted Weems's Sobbin' Blues and in vaudeville.

segments.chapter: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
segments.title: His bag of tricks and how jazz noises came from the theater
segments.summary: Zutty lists the gong, auto horn and duck call he used in theaters and big bands. He and Dance agree the novelty noises in early jazz came from theater work, not dance halls.

segments.chapter: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
segments.title: Ethel Waters, the Lyric Theater and John Robichaux
segments.summary: Marge says Ethel Waters claimed she brought Zutty out of New Orleans; Zutty says she taught him the Charleston at the theater. He worked the Lyric with Robichaux only after leaving the Cadillac, and after the Navy.

segments.chapter: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
segments.title: Joining the Navy at seventeen
segments.summary: Zutty joined the Navy because he admired the clean-looking sailors; his mother had to sign and Marge says he also loved travel and adventure.

segments.chapter: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
segments.title: The Savoy Ballroom: dancing, Count Basie and the bouncers
segments.summary: Zutty and Marge recall Ethel Waters and Louis dancing at the Savoy, taking Jimmy Dorsey there, and Count Basie asking if he would beat him to Europe. The bouncers were ex-fighters.

segments.chapter: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
segments.title: Spoiled and free: his mother's attitude
segments.summary: His mother let him do what he wanted during the war; Marge says he was spoiled but carries no chip on his shoulder.

segments.chapter: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
segments.title: Chauffeuring after the Navy; his mother the cook and Tuskegee
segments.summary: After the Navy Zutty drove a Cadillac for a family. His mother cooked for Madame Le Jeune, who wanted him to finish school so she could send him to Tuskegee.

segments.chapter: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
segments.title: Regret at not having a proper education
segments.summary: Zutty regrets his lack of schooling; Marge mentions a woman with degrees, and a professor's wife tells him his drumming needs no education. Dance agrees schooling might have changed his playing.

segments.chapter: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
segments.title: Riding the rails to Chicago as a loner
segments.summary: Zutty says he was a loner, going into the woods with a stick, and tells how he asked an engineer to let him shovel coal to Chicago and walked through a yard of railroad detectives.

segments.chapter: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
segments.title: Marge's sweetheart Jerome Pasquall, the educated saxophonist
segments.summary: Marge tells how Jerome Pasquall, her saxophone-playing sweetheart in her brother's St. Louis band, studied in Chicago and Boston, got a music degree, then ended up in New York's unemployment office, having respelled his name.

segments.chapter: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
segments.title: Zutty can read and write; Marge handles the business
segments.summary: Marge says people wrongly thought Zutty could not read or write; he wrote well until his stroke. She has always handled his union business and contracts, as she did for her brother.

segments.chapter: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
segments.title: Marge's account books and Nick's back pay
segments.summary: When Nick owed the band months of pay, Marge came with her ledgers and collected, impressing Nick. Zutty says that is why she is with him.

segments.chapter: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
segments.title: Firing Hank Duncan at Nick's
segments.summary: Zutty fired the drunk pianist Hank Duncan, who changed key behind Edmond Hall. Marge met Hank at the union, where he had filed charges for lack of notice, and got him to withdraw them.

segments.chapter: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
segments.title: Replacements at the piano: Big Boy and Gene Anderson
segments.summary: Zutty brought in a huge pianist called Big Boy, who later went to Canada; when Big Boy left for an act he got Gene Anderson, formerly of the Carroll Dickerson band.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, Louis and the Lyric
segments.title: Tom's Road House, a fight over food and Bootsy Hernandez
segments.summary: Zutty replaced Little Joe Lindsey at Tom's Road House with Big Eye Louis, but was fired over a scuffle with the head waiter about food. Bootsy Hernandez then offered him a job at Archie's Cabaret.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, Louis and the Lyric
segments.title: Hiring Louis Armstrong for the Orchard Cabaret
segments.summary: Zutty hired Louis, Johnny St. Cyr and Yudell Wilson for the Orchard; Bootsy Hernandez, a Manuel Perez fan, loved Louis. Zutty says Louis played very well.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, Louis and the Lyric
segments.title: Fletcher Henderson's telegram and Louis leaving for King Oliver
segments.summary: Louis showed Zutty Fletcher Henderson's telegram and refused to go without him; Fletcher had Kaiser Marshall. Louis later left for King Oliver, and Buster Bailey got him the Henderson job.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, Louis and the Lyric
segments.title: Baby Dodds and Red Happy's drum contest
segments.summary: Zutty knew Baby Dodds in New Orleans; Dodds and Red Happy had a drumming contest on Zutty's drums, and a Preservation Hall drummer says he learned from Red Happy.
