segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, Louis and the Lyric
segments.title: Drummers who influenced him: Louis Cottrell and Paul Detroit
segments.summary: Zutty names Louis Cottrell Sr. and Paul Detroit as his models, admiring their tone and tuning; he says Paul Barbarin was just ahead of him and mentions Henry Martin.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, Louis and the Lyric
segments.title: Zutty's love of the theater and segregated seating in St. Louis
segments.summary: Marge says Zutty always loved theaters and took her to shows in St. Louis, while she was bitter at having to sit upstairs. Dance praises his attitude.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, Louis and the Lyric
segments.title: Zutty the gentleman: finer things, horse shows
segments.summary: Marge says musicians are wrongly pictured as drunkards; Zutty was neat and gentlemanly and took her to Madison Square Garden horse shows.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, Louis and the Lyric
segments.title: Seeing Count Basie and Lovie Taylor's dancing in St. Louis shows
segments.summary: In St. Louis they saw Count Basie with Gonzelle White on the burlesque wheel, plus Rose Marie and Chu Chin Chow. Jasper Taylor's drumming in Joe Jordan's band backed the soft-shoe dancer Lovie Taylor.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, Louis and the Lyric
segments.title: Zutty was not a gambler; sports; tape pause
segments.summary: Marge says Zutty did not gamble but liked theater and ball games. Dance notes the session was delayed for the World Series and plans a new tape.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, Louis and the Lyric
segments.title: The Cadillac Cafe band with Albert Nicholas and Lee Collins
segments.summary: After the Orchard, Zutty moved to the Cadillac Cafe with Albert Nicholas, Lee Collins and Lu Russell. They discuss Lee Collins, who sounded like Louis but skipped bars and was loved in Europe.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, Louis and the Lyric
segments.title: Getting the John Robichaux job at the Lyric Theater
segments.summary: Robichaux heard Zutty from outside the Cadillac and hired him; Willie Jackson and another rehearsed him on the chorus-girl kicks. The Lyric stood at Burgundy Street and shone a light on him.

segments.chapter: New Orleans bands, Louis and the Lyric
segments.title: Duplicated re-typing of pages 49-54
segments.summary: This run repeats the text of the earlier pages almost word for word (Lovie Taylor, gambling, the Cadillac, Lee Collins, Robichaux and the Lyric) and ends Tape 1.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Tape 2 begins; the dog Breakdown and Kay Kyser
segments.summary: Tape 2 opens in Washington in May 1975. Zutty and Marge recall their dog of seventeen years who woofed when a musician missed a note on a Kay Kyser broadcast, and Dance tells of Tuff Jordan's dog liking Louis Armstrong.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: First seeing Gene Krupa as a kid outside Jeffrey Tavern
segments.summary: Playing Jeffrey Tavern on the South Side, Zutty saw a young face listening at the window; Mezz Mezzrow later introduced Gene Krupa at the Savoy, and Zutty recognized him.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Vernon Roulette's band at Jeffrey Tavern and Doc Cook's offer
segments.summary: Zutty played about a year at Jeffrey Tavern in the Carroll Dickerson-style band with Earl Hines briefly on piano, until Doc Cook hired him and an altoist for Harmon's Dreamland.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: First regular Chicago job; Marge's jealousy and manicuring
segments.summary: Marge recalls Zutty's first Chicago job, her jealousy and her work as a manicurist in a friend's shop, which kept them going for months during the three-month union wait.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Subbing for Baby Dodds at Kelly's Stables
segments.summary: Zutty explains he first worked in Chicago when Baby Dodds laid off a night at Kelly's Stables, where tips were so good he took home over seventeen dollars. Dance stresses it was a high-class place.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: The Jeffrey Tavern band and singer Ellen Savage
segments.summary: Zutty describes the band at Jeffrey Tavern: three saxes, four rhythm, two trumpets and a trombone, playing a show with the shouting singer Ellen Savage.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Lyric Theatre vaudeville training and Fate Marable's invitation
segments.summary: Zutty says his show experience came from the Lyric Theatre in New Orleans, where Willie Jackson taught him the chorus-girl steps and he bought effects. Leaving there, Fate Marable called him onto the boat, the conservatory.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Marable's band on the St. Paul versus Buffano's on the J.S.
segments.summary: Marable's band was on the St. Paul and Jules Buffano's, with Wayne King, on the J.S. The Streckfus brothers sent the society crowd to the J.S. and the ordinary crowd to the St. Paul.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: How the riverboats ran, and Little Eva Talbot's frat parties
segments.summary: Summers the boat was in St. Louis, winters in New Orleans, with evening excursions leaving around eight. Little Eva Talbot, a Tulane football star, booked the band for fraternity parties.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Marable's band lineup, repertoire and its two pianists
segments.summary: The Marable band had three saxes, banjo, four rhythm, trombone, two trumpets and a violin. It played popular tunes and waltzes, copied from records; Fate himself and Loving Good played piano.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Meeting Charlie Creath and Marge shooting dice
segments.summary: Zutty met Charlie Creath in Louisville at Derby time; in St. Louis he went to Creath's house and met Marge on the floor shooting dice with the band.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Marge's piano playing and Club 47 in California
segments.summary: Zutty says Marge played well in the band, and Doc Randall and Nappy Lamare, owners of Club 47 in Los Angeles, praised her walking-bass left hand when she sat in.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Charlie Creath's reputation, Dago Hill and his mute playing
segments.summary: Creath was a big man on Dago Hill and made the rounds of several bands a night. He loved mutes and had circus training with the Ringling Brothers band.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Charlie Creath's death in 1951
segments.summary: On the way to Europe in 1951 they visited Charlie, then got a telegram on the boat saying he was dead. In Paris his wife wrote that he killed himself over a bookmaking debt.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Creath after they left St. Louis
segments.summary: The Singletons left St. Louis in 1925; Creath kept bands going about five years and then played on boats. They passed through Pittsburgh in a 1936 Ford without finding him.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Marge's piano lessons, ragtime and East St. Louis
segments.summary: Marge studied piano for three years by the Czerny method and learned ragtime from Frank Eubanks, who learned it from Jelly Roll Morton. They clarify that East St. Louis is across the bridge in Illinois.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Marge's nurse training and her brother putting her in the band
segments.summary: Marge quit nurse training after a quarrel with a supervisor, so her brother Charlie made her play piano in his dance band, starting at the Almac dance hall.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: The six-piece band and the name Jazz-O-Maniacs
segments.summary: At 19 Marge played in Charlie's six-piece band; as jazz came in he named it Charlie Creath and his Jazz-O-Maniacs.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Italian dancers, and the first Black band in a white hall on Pine Street
segments.summary: White Italian youths from Dago Hill began coming to the Black dance hall and then hired Creath for a white hall on Pine Street, a first for a Black band in segregated St. Louis.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Red McKenzie and the future Mound City Blue Blowers sitting in
segments.summary: Bellhops Red McKenzie, Jack Bland and Dick Slevin came to sit in with combs and a banjo, getting experience with Creath before becoming the Mound City Blue Blowers.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Frankie Trumbauer and the white bands at West Lake
segments.summary: Trumbauer, in a society band at the Arcadia, had Creath's band play there for a night, and Creath then played West Lake in summers alternating with a white band including Bix and Pee Wee.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: The mixed benefit band at the Booker Washington Theatre
segments.summary: Zutty and Creath invited the white West Lake musicians, including Pee Wee Russell and Bix, to play a benefit at the Booker Washington Theatre; Zutty thinks it was his first mixed band.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Creath the star trumpeter and Marge running his business
segments.summary: Creath made one appearance at several gigs a night and sent other bands, and in St. Louis was thought the greatest trumpeter. Marge handled his contracts and books as he gambled.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Meeting Marge: love at first sight
segments.summary: Zutty recounts again meeting Charlie and Marge on the way to St. Louis with Marable's band after the Louisville derby ball; Marge says something hit her when she looked up.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Marge's season on the St. Paul with Charlie's band
segments.summary: Charlie was hired for a season on the St. Paul and insisted the Streckfus brothers take Marge as pianist, though they wanted a stronger player. They came to like her.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Shy young Louis Armstrong on the boat
segments.summary: Marge met a shy Louis Armstrong on Marable's boat, who ran from the girls to the water fountain; Zutty adds he collected gum wrappers and spilled his olives in the station.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Charlie Creath's background: Professor Bowles, the circus and her brother
segments.summary: Marge explains Charlie learned to read in Professor Bowles's high-school band, joined P.G. Lowry's circus band at 17 and took up trumpet after their older brother died of scarlet fever.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: St. Louis trumpeters and the Masonic band training
segments.summary: Other trumpeters like Eddie Allen and George Jackson could not draw crowds; St. Louis musicians all read, trained in the Masonic bands under Old Man Langford, as Clark Terry and Shorty Baker later did.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Northern popular style and Creath's blues
segments.summary: Creath's band played northern stock orchestrations in the style of Isham Jones and Paul Whiteman, not New Orleans style, but Creath was famed as a soulful blues player.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Creath hears Zutty, who returns to St. Louis and joins him
segments.summary: Creath came back from the Derby raving about a drummer called Singleton, to the annoyance of his drummers. Zutty went home to New Orleans, missed Marge and joined Creath for about a year and a half.

segments.chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
segments.title: Falling out with Charlie and deciding to go to Chicago
segments.summary: After a disagreement and over Creath's objection, the newly married Singletons left for Chicago in a Model T; Zutty wanted bigger things and knew the New Orleans musicians there.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York shows, 1925-33
segments.title: The Model T drive to Chicago
segments.summary: The drive took a day or two, sleeping in the car and losing half a day to repairs after the generator burned out.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York shows, 1925-33
segments.title: Tape 3 begins with the trip lines repeated
segments.summary: Tape 3 header and a re-run of the car-trip exchange, followed by a gap in the tape.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York shows, 1925-33
segments.title: Don Redman, built up by Zutty and finally seen
segments.summary: Marge recalls Zutty praising Don Redman's arranging in Chicago, and meeting him in New York outside the Lafayette, where he turned out to be a small man in knickers and a Panama hat.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York shows, 1925-33
segments.title: Naming the records: West End Blues and Knee Drops
segments.summary: Dance asks about the meaning of titles; Zutty says Knee Drops and Knocking the Jug were named in the studio, and Louis was thrilled to see his name in lights at the Savoy.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York shows, 1925-33
segments.title: Louis the humble man, and his last days in hospital
segments.summary: Marge says Louis stayed down to earth, amazed at the limousine, and was closest to Zutty. In his last days Louis asked for Zutty at the hospital, where they sat with him.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York shows, 1925-33
segments.title: The private tape of Louis and Zutty reminiscing
segments.summary: Louis and Zutty made a private tape at the Alvin Hotel where he talked about Punch Miller, and Louis played Zutty's records and told his chauffeur how Zutty could push a band.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York shows, 1925-33
segments.title: Big bands and shows versus small groups
segments.summary: Dance notes Zutty's early career was in big bands and shows, harder work; Zutty recalls the Connie's Inn show and how his Lyric Theater experience helped him catch dancers' moves with the ratchet.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York shows, 1925-33
segments.title: Knee Drops as a dance step, and Gene Krupa's love of the record
segments.summary: Zutty explains Knee Drops was a dance in which dancers dropped to their knees, and says Gene Krupa loved the tune; a fellow told him the record is in the Smithsonian.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York shows, 1925-33
segments.title: Leading his own band at the Lafayette Theatre
segments.summary: Zutty led his own band in a show at the Lafayette, with Tom Whaley conducting instead of Donald Haywood, Bubber Miley on trumpet and Gene Anderson on piano; Nina Mae McKinney hit an actor with a gun that jammed.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York shows, 1925-33
segments.title: Norman and Arlene Selby's blackface Louis act
segments.summary: After the Renaissance with Vernon Andrade, Zutty went to Philadelphia and Chicago with Norman and Arlene Selby, whose act had Norman impersonating Louis Armstrong on trumpet.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York shows, 1925-33
segments.title: Fats Waller's big band at Connie's Inn
segments.summary: Zutty returned to Connie's Inn with a big band led by Fats Waller, who played organ and piano, playing all of Fats's tunes.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York shows, 1925-33
segments.title: The Follies Bergere in Chicago with Sally Rand
segments.summary: In Chicago in 1933 Zutty played the Selby act in the Follies Bergere floor show, sitting in the band beside George Wettling, with Sally Rand and Joe E. Lewis in the show.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York shows, 1925-33
segments.title: Sid Catlett recommends Zutty to the Selbys
segments.summary: The Selbys got Zutty through Sid Catlett, who could not take the job; they work out which band Catlett was with in New York at the time.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York shows, 1925-33
segments.title: The Berry Brothers act at the Paramount with Tommy Ladnier
segments.summary: Zutty and Tommy Ladnier played the pit for the Berry Brothers act at the Paramount, then Brooklyn and Providence, and Joe Jordan used the union delegate threat to get the locked pit doors opened.

segments.chapter: Ladnier, Bechet and Zutty's loyalties
segments.title: The House of Meditation: Bechet and Ladnier's classical-only flat
segments.summary: Zutty hung out at 129th and Seventh in the place Bechet and Ladnier lived, where only classical records played and a picture of Beethoven hung; Ladnier told Bechet he was the image of Beethoven.

segments.chapter: Ladnier, Bechet and Zutty's loyalties
segments.title: Ladnier's fish club names and Louis's reaction
segments.summary: Ladnier and Bechet were seriously Rosicrucian. Ladnier ran a fish club, naming himself King Fish and others Minnow and Black Bass, and Zutty thinks Louis disliked being named the Viper Fish.

segments.chapter: Ladnier, Bechet and Zutty's loyalties
segments.title: Ladnier's Rosicrucian withdrawal from music
segments.summary: Marge says Ladnier tried to explain Rosicrucianism to them on Seventh Avenue and wanted to be alone, stopped caring about his appearance and family, and one of his last jobs was the Panassie date.

segments.chapter: Ladnier, Bechet and Zutty's loyalties
segments.title: The Panassie session, drunk piano and Viva La France
segments.summary: Zutty recounts the Panassie session in which Ladnier got James P. Johnson so drunk he could not play, and Ladnier cheered up the sad Frenchman by saying Viva La France.

segments.chapter: Ladnier, Bechet and Zutty's loyalties
segments.title: Ladnier's death at Mezz's house
segments.summary: Ladnier died at Mezz Mezzrow's house with a pad and pencil in hand. Zutty and Buck Washington, who lived in the Singletons' building on 47th Street, went there.

segments.chapter: Ladnier, Bechet and Zutty's loyalties
segments.title: Bechet the thinker, and the classics at the House of Meditation
segments.summary: Zutty insists Bechet and Ladnier were deep in the Rosicrucian beliefs and spoke the same language; Bechet knew stories like the swan and no jazz records were played.

segments.chapter: Ladnier, Bechet and Zutty's loyalties
segments.title: Bechet at Nick's and getting Zutty out
segments.summary: Zutty got Bechet in at Nick's, where Nick disliked the fish horn, and Bechet later wanted the Spirits of Rhythm out and Zutty fired. Marge says he wanted to be the star and was mean.

segments.chapter: Ladnier, Bechet and Zutty's loyalties
segments.title: Bechet's demanding letter from Paris
segments.summary: Bechet wrote to Zutty at the Alvin Hotel to join him in the Band Box with a long list of dos and don'ts; Marge tore it up. Dance adds that in the 1930s people called Bechet's vibrato corny.

segments.chapter: Ladnier, Bechet and Zutty's loyalties
segments.title: The overcoat and the breakfasts Marge cooked for Bechet
segments.summary: Zutty fed Bechet and gave him an overcoat, and Marge complains about cooking him breakfast and dinner and shucking his corn; Zutty hid the coat one night when Bechet was nasty and then gave it back.

segments.chapter: Ladnier, Bechet and Zutty's loyalties
segments.title: Bechet selfish; his villa and soprano-horn car in France
segments.summary: Zutty and Marge say Bechet could not be trusted and was selfish, yet in France he invited them and Lil Armstrong to his villa in Lille and drove them in a car whose horn played a saxophone riff.

segments.chapter: Ladnier, Bechet and Zutty's loyalties
segments.title: Loving the music regardless of the person; Zutty's color-blindness
segments.summary: Dance and Paul Gonsalves say you may love someone's music whatever his character; Marge says Zutty never saw color and treated white musicians as friends.

segments.chapter: Ladnier, Bechet and Zutty's loyalties
segments.title: Getting Mel Powell started at Nick's
segments.summary: Zutty brought the white pianist Mel Powell to play at Nick's, and Nick objected to a white boy with a Black band, so Zutty let him play one night and told Nick it was him, not the customers.

segments.chapter: Ladnier, Bechet and Zutty's loyalties
segments.title: Jess Stacy and Joe Sullivan, musicians who became loners
segments.summary: Dance wonders why Jess Stacy gave up; Zutty says musicians turn loner like Joe Sullivan, who wanted to host them in California but Zutty had too many friends to see.

segments.chapter: Ladnier, Bechet and Zutty's loyalties
segments.title: The English drummer and the Frankfurt benefit
segments.summary: Zutty once gave ten dollars to a young English drummer at Ryan's, and after Zutty's stroke the drummer organized a benefit in Frankfurt and sent a check for almost five hundred dollars.

segments.chapter: Ladnier, Bechet and Zutty's loyalties
segments.title: Remembering names and faces
segments.summary: Dance and the Singletons talk about the strain of remembering so many people; Louis said no one had a memory like Zutty's for names.

segments.chapter: Ladnier, Bechet and Zutty's loyalties
segments.title: Pike Davis's band behind Bill Robinson, and the Yankee Stadium job
segments.summary: Backing Bill Robinson at the Lafayette, Zutty fell through the drums. Robinson then hired his band for the Black Yankees game, tried to avoid paying, and gave the road job to Cab Calloway.

segments.chapter: Ladnier, Bechet and Zutty's loyalties
segments.title: Joe Glaser, Cozy Cole's pay and the Armstrong band
segments.summary: Joe Glaser called Zutty a horse's ass for asking the same money as Cozy Cole and never hired him for Armstrong's band; Zutty also tells of Rex Stewart's night at the Lenox Club.

segments.chapter: Ladnier, Bechet and Zutty's loyalties
segments.title: Armstrong's later drummers
segments.summary: Dance and the Singletons list the drummers Louis had later, such as Barrett Deems and Danny Barcelona, which Dance calls stupid.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Correcting the biography: the Fair, Dickerson and the dates
segments.summary: Dance reads the career summary; Zutty places the Follies Bergere at the Chicago fair and says he last played with Carroll Dickerson in New York in 1929, when Louis quit.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: The New Deal Club on the West Side
segments.summary: Zutty describes the New Deal Club, a rough West Side joint run by Charlie with gangsters' sons, where Marge once filled in on piano with her long fingernails.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: The Three Deuces: his band, Roy Eldridge and Art Tatum
segments.summary: At the Three Deuces until about 1937 Zutty led his band, then Roy Eldridge joined after the flood and Art Tatum took over; the earlier records were made before Roy.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Tape 4 begins; why they went to Chicago
segments.summary: A new reel header (reels 4-6) opens with Dance asking why Zutty went to Chicago, where many New Orleans musicians were, and returning to the Roulette band and the Kelly's Stable job.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Doc Cook's offer and the saxophonist Billy Butler
segments.summary: Doc Cook took Zutty and the alto saxophonist Billy Butler, who Marge says now holds a city job; Zutty adds King Oliver once had him direct his band.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: A different car trip and the cows on the road
segments.summary: Marge corrects that the generator trouble was on another trip; on a drive in a big red Peerless with Charlie Creath, Zutty dozed at the wheel and hit a herd of cows, breaking one cow's leg.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Doc Cook's demand for a huge bass drum at Dreamland
segments.summary: Doc Cook wanted a big old-style bass drum for volume at Harmon's Dreamland; Zutty, with new drums, refused and they had a falling out.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Doubling at the Nest with Jimmy Noone and Jerome Carrington
segments.summary: After Dreamland Zutty doubled at the Nest, an after-hours club, with Jimmy Noone and the pianist Jerome Carrington. They played until ten or eleven in the morning, with Bud Freeman, Eddie Condon and Benny Goodman coming by.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Doc Cook, doctor of music and his Seventeen Interns
segments.summary: Zutty laughs that he still talked with Doc Cook about the bass drum on Broadway; Cook held a music doctorate and led Doc Cook and His Seventeen Interns.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: The Nest's clientele and splitting the tips three ways
segments.summary: The Nest drew society and big-time pimps; the three-man band split large tips evenly, Zutty bringing home piles of cash. Carrington was last seen in Washington in 1946.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Jimmy Noone: his death, golf, family and California
segments.summary: Zutty praised Jimmy Noone, who died on the way to an Orson Welles broadcast rehearsal, loved California and golf, and had children by a second marriage.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Marge gave up the piano for home
segments.summary: Marge stopped playing because Zutty was jealous and she did not want to ride in cars of band members; she stayed home and cared for him, and that, she says, is why they stayed together.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Seven nights a week at the Nest
segments.summary: Zutty worked seven nights a week, slept all day, wore only a tuxedo, and he and Marge rarely got to a show or movie.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Show people at the Nest, and Louis and Hines opening the Sunset
segments.summary: Zutty names theatrical visitors, including Carl Sandburg; King Oliver wanted Louis at the Plantation but Louis opened at the Sunset across the street, with Earl Hines.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Kelly's Stables with Baby Dodds, before the union card
segments.summary: Zutty explains Kelly's was a small gig that the New Orleans boys gave him before his union wait ended, with Charlie Alexander and Dominique in the group.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Dave Peyton's band at the Cafe de Paris
segments.summary: After Doc Cook, Zutty played with Dave Peyton at the Cafe de Paris, a big nightclub where Ethel Waters opened a show and Sophie Tucker and Vincent Lopez came.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Clarence Jones's band at the Metropolitan Theater with Louis
segments.summary: With Jimmy Noone at the Nest, Zutty joined pianist Clarence Jones at the Metropolitan Theater, a movie house where he and Louis did an act and he wore a dress for a comic number.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Louis and Earl Hines at the Warwick Hall; leaving Noone for Dickerson
segments.summary: Zutty tells of the short Warwick Hall venture with Louis and Hines, and of leaving Jimmy Noone and the Apex to join Carroll Dickerson at the Savoy.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Warwick Hall flops against the new Savoy ballroom
segments.summary: The six-piece band with Louis, Hines and Lil as agent did no business at the old Warwick Hall, while the new Savoy on South Parkway drew the crowds; a jealous husband once pulled a pistol on the band.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Joining Carroll Dickerson's band and coming to New York
segments.summary: After the Warwick flop Zutty went into the Apex, then the Savoy with Carroll Dickerson's band featuring Louis, and they came to New York together, a stint of almost two years.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Filling in for Ellington at the Audubon Theatre
segments.summary: In New York the band first opened at the Savoy, then took Duke's place at the Audubon Theatre in the Bronx, where Louis's St. Louis Blues high notes made the pit orchestra stand up.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Louis, Zutty and the choice between friendship and business
segments.summary: Louis asked Zutty to stay with him, but Zutty had a Connie's Inn offer and told Louis friendship is one thing and business another; Mezz's book says he cut out from Louis.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: The failed Ziegfeld audition
segments.summary: The band auditioned for a Ziegfeld show, which Duke Ellington got, but Ziegfeld walked out on them.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Connie's Inn under Allie Ross and the WOR commercial program
segments.summary: Zutty went into Connie's Inn with Allie Ross's band and had one of the first commercial radio programs by a Black band, on WOR for a clothing store. Marge and Zutty argue whether it was Dickerson's men.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Louis leaves Dickerson's band and joins Luis Russell
segments.summary: Louis left Connie's Inn and the Dickerson band without warning, leaving the men stranded and short of fare to Chicago, and joined Luis Russell's band, booked by Rockwell.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: The Luis Russell band behind Louis
segments.summary: Marge says Russell's was the worst band, unlike Dickerson's, whose men played like a choir behind Louis; at Loew's State Louis told Zutty he did not even hear them.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Allie Ross's band: LeRoy Smith's men
segments.summary: Zutty says Allie Ross's band grew from LeRoy Smith's band, a good band whose men doubled on many instruments, with a Puerto Rican bassist and three Puerto Rican violinists.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Joe Glaser opens the Sunset and bills Louis the World's Greatest Trumpeter
segments.summary: Back in Chicago Zutty was doubling with Doc Cook while Joe Glaser opened the Sunset and first billed Louis Armstrong as World's Greatest Trumpeter.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Hot Chocolates: Louis keeps Zutty at Connie's Inn
segments.summary: Dance says Hot Chocolates and Ain't Misbehavin' marked Louis's commercial rise; Zutty was wanted for the Broadway show but Louis told him to stay and take care of the Connie's Inn band.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Lucille's claim that Zutty took a band from Louis
segments.summary: Marge reports Lucille said Louis never hired Zutty because he would not have another band taken from him; Marge and Dance insist the Dickerson band simply broke up and Zutty stayed at Connie's Inn.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Hot Chocolates and Connie's Inn: the shows and Louis's jealousy
segments.summary: Zutty played in pit bands, not as soloist; Louis did the Broadway show then returned to Connie's Inn, singing Black and Blue. Marge says friends believed Louis was jealous of Zutty's popularity with the show girls.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Earl Hines goes off to lead his own band
segments.summary: Earl Hines left Louis to lead his own band at the Grand Terrace, and Gene Anderson took the piano in Dickerson's band at the Savoy.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Zutty would have quit any band to play with Louis; Louis's devotion
segments.summary: Marge says Zutty would have given up anything to play with Louis, who loved him back and nursed him after his stroke, saying he'd kill himself if Zutty died.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Louis in Chick Webb's band and the sore lip
segments.summary: After Russell, Louis went with Chick Webb's band, which was wrong for him, with jealous trumpeters, and strain on his lip from nightly high notes forced him to lay off for about a year.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Chick Webb the arrangement drummer versus New Orleans drumming
segments.summary: Zutty calls Chick Webb a big-time arrangement drummer, an early band drummer respected by Duke; Zutty always played for the soloist, the New Orleans way, a difference audible on Webb's records.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Zutty never recorded with Louis except Dickerson and Chicago sessions
segments.summary: They agree Zutty never made a full record date with Louis other than the Carroll Dickerson band, When You're Smiling, and the Chicago small-group sides such as Skip the Gutter and Knee Drops.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Lil Armstrong and Rockwell steer Louis toward money
segments.summary: Marge says Lil wanted Louis to commercialize, and was unhappy to see them the night Zutty confronted Louis; Lil said she would straighten the record in her book but never did.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: The William Morris office and Zutty's lack of interest in money
segments.summary: In California the William Morris office got Zutty movie bits, but he turned down the road; Pat Rodkin got him a thousand dollars when he would have taken $350, and he refused Joe Sullivan and Pee Wee Russell's calls to return East.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Making the Chicago records: West End Blues and the studio
segments.summary: They rehearsed in Lil's front room on her new baby grand, Hines and Jelly Roll loved the piano, and titles were often invented in the studio, which had burlap sacks hanging on the walls.

segments.chapter: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
segments.title: Don Redman arranging for Louis in Chicago
segments.summary: Louis wanted Don Redman, then handling the Gold Coast Kette bands out of McKinney's Cotton Pickers, to write arrangements for the band; the tape ends.

segments.chapter: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
segments.title: Chicago gangster hangouts and the New Deal Club
segments.summary: Chicago meant seeing nothing; Zutty played Greenwood Gardens, a hangout of Capone's brother. He retells how Marge filled in at the New Deal Club, with Reuben Reeves, the gangsters' sons and no shooting.

segments.chapter: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
segments.title: Jazz slang: bring down, drag, swing them into bad health
segments.summary: Marge and Dance trade slang such as bring down, drag and swinging them into bad health, and Paul Gonsalves objecting to calling someone a drag.

segments.chapter: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
segments.title: The dog Bring Down bought at Westchester
segments.summary: Marge says Bring Down is named for spending six of ten dollars on the dog when she needed the rent; Zutty bought him while playing at Westchester with Hawk, Hot Lips, Pee Wee and Fats.

segments.chapter: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
segments.title: Two years at the Lyric Theater among the vaudeville acts
segments.summary: Zutty played the Lyric about two years, knowing Ethel Waters, Bessie Smith, Bruce's grocery store tab show, Butter Beans and Susie, and a dancer compared to Bojangles.

segments.chapter: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
segments.title: Ethel Waters and the four-in-a-bar Charleston; Tim Moore
segments.summary: Zutty says Ethel Waters taught him the Charleston singing James P. Johnson's tune; he could not manage two in a bar, so played four in a bar. Tim Moore's boxing act with a midget is recalled.

segments.chapter: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
segments.title: First trip to Chicago as a boy via the railroad pass
segments.summary: At sixteen Zutty left New Orleans with friends on a railroad work pass, got off at Clinton, Illinois, rode in a coal bin to Chicago, walked through the yards and met Red Ernest's family at 35th and State.

segments.chapter: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
segments.title: Tony Jackson and the piano players of New Orleans' 25 club
segments.summary: He went to Chicago wanting to hear Tony Jackson, whose fame he knew from the '25' where New Orleans piano players and pimps hung out. Marge never heard Jackson.

segments.chapter: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
segments.title: Why women went for musicians
segments.summary: Marge and Dance consider why good musicians were also pimps: women always liked musicians, who had money and glamour, as Bud Freeman's story shows.

segments.chapter: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
segments.title: Musicians' dress then and now
segments.summary: Dance and Marge note musicians in the old days were sharp dressers in tie and white shirt, whereas today they look like they came off the farm.

segments.chapter: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
segments.title: Madames' stables of girls and the welcoming committees
segments.summary: Marge explains that in New Orleans and East St. Louis madams brought their girls to dances to meet musicians, later replaced by the young welcoming committees of Basie's day.

segments.chapter: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
segments.title: Hearing Tony Jackson at the Deluxe Cafe
segments.summary: Red Batiste took Zutty to hear Tony Jackson upstairs at the Deluxe Cafe in Chicago, playing beautiful non-jazz music such as Pretty Baby.

segments.chapter: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
segments.title: Jelly Roll's respect for Jackson; Lizzie Miles
segments.summary: Zutty says Jelly Roll respected Tony Jackson; Dance asks about Lizzie Miles, who came along about then, was good but a little different from Bessie Smith, and later sang with Bob Scobey.

segments.chapter: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
segments.title: Staying in Chicago until the snow and sending home for fare
segments.summary: As a boy Zutty drifted about Chicago until the first snow scared him and he wired home for the $25.65 fare, then joined the Navy the next summer.

segments.chapter: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
segments.title: Correcting the order: Lyric, then Marable's boat, then St. Louis
segments.summary: Dance corrects the bio: Zutty went from the Orchard and Cadillac to the Lyric, was hired out of the Lyric by Fate Marable, then left the boats and went back to the Lyric before Creath called him.

segments.chapter: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
segments.title: Who was in Fate Marable's band when Zutty joined
segments.summary: Zutty lists Sidney Desvignes and Amos White on trumpets, a trombonist named Brashear, three saxes, bass, banjo and a Paducah violinist, with Loving Good later added as second pianist.

segments.chapter: Chicago memories and the road to the Navy
segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton, respected and boastful
segments.summary: Zutty says Jelly Roll was respected though people gave him hell for bragging; his claims to know where Tiger Rag came from were credible.

segments.chapter: Zutty's stroke and friends
segments.title: The stroke the day after Christmas 1969
segments.summary: After Dance asks about the last years, the Jazz Fest in New Orleans in June 1969, Zutty describes waking with a numb foot and sensing a stroke after a fine family dinner.

segments.chapter: Zutty's stroke and friends
segments.title: A dizzy spell in the five-and-ten a week earlier
segments.summary: Marge recalls Zutty nearly fainted buying wrapping paper at the five-and-ten a week before, which they put down to heat; the cause was hypertension they didn't know he had.

segments.chapter: Zutty's stroke and friends
segments.title: No check-ups, and Dr. MacDonald
segments.summary: They hadn't seen a doctor in years; the last, Dr. MacDonald, who also treated Pee Wee Russell, told Zutty to put on his clothes and get out, and Dance is offered cakes.

segments.chapter: Zutty's stroke and friends
segments.title: Marge's closed esophagus and the operation
segments.summary: Through Dick Kennedy they got Dr. MacDonald for Marge, whose esophagus had completely closed from nervous tension that began in Europe; an operation at St. Clare's saved her.

segments.chapter: Zutty's stroke and friends
segments.title: Marshall Brown's loudspeakers blamed for the hypertension
segments.summary: Marge believes the loud electronic equipment Marshall Brown placed next to Zutty's drums at his job, leaving him unable to hear, raised his blood pressure.

segments.chapter: Zutty's stroke and friends
segments.title: Quarrel with Max Kaminsky over the amplifier and quitting
segments.summary: Zutty complained to Max Kaminsky, who promised to turn the speaker down but made it louder; Zutty called him a phony and left. A Notre Dame bandleader sympathized, and Marge had begged him to quit.

segments.chapter: Zutty's stroke and friends
segments.title: Staggering in California before the stroke
segments.summary: Marge recalls that on a trip to Berkeley a friend noticed Zutty staggering as he walked, probably the stroke coming on.

segments.chapter: Zutty's stroke and friends
segments.title: Waiting hours at the Veterans' Hospital
segments.summary: After Dr. Murphy suggested the Veterans' Hospital, Marge got Zutty there by cab in snow and ice and they waited from 2:30 to 8 pm; the neurologist found a clot on the left side, a slight stroke.

segments.chapter: Zutty's stroke and friends
segments.title: Refusing the spinal tap and nursing him at home
segments.summary: Marge refused the spinal tap and took Zutty home despite the hospital's anger, kept him on a salt-free diet with Dr. Newman, though they first ate Chinese food, and Zutty was told not to drink.

segments.chapter: Zutty's stroke and friends
segments.title: Belkis Ertegun's chauffeured Rolls Royce to the doctor
segments.summary: Marge called Belkis Ertegun about getting Zutty through the snow to the doctor and the next day a chauffeured Rolls Royce arrived, with daughter Alma along.

segments.chapter: Zutty's stroke and friends
segments.title: The friendship with Nesuhi Ertegun from 1939
segments.summary: Dance asks where the friendship began; Zutty says from Nick's in 1939, when they played the Press Club in Washington for Nesuhi, whose father was the Turkish Ambassador.

segments.chapter: Zutty's stroke and friends
segments.title: Marge nursing Zutty at home, with Alma's help
segments.summary: Marge cared for Zutty at home rather than a hospital, keeping him quiet on a salt-free diet; their daughter Alma, a nursing supervisor, took his blood pressure daily.

segments.chapter: Zutty's stroke and friends
segments.title: Rehabilitation, the Alvin Hotel move and Atlantic's help
segments.summary: Nesuhi's car took Zutty to therapy for two years at the French Hospital, and Atlantic Records paid for moving them from the Alvin to the Woodward without letting Marge lift a thing.

segments.chapter: Zutty's stroke and friends
segments.title: Taking John Hammond to hear Meade Lux Lewis
segments.summary: Zutty and George Wettling took John Hammond to a South Parkway flat to hear Meade Lux Lewis, who was washing cars, which is how Hammond got to Meade Lux.

segments.chapter: Zutty's stroke and friends
segments.title: Nesuhi pays for a Caribbean cruise with spending money
segments.summary: When Zutty wished he could give Marge a trip, Ertegun offered to pay, booking a first-class cruise plus a thousand dollars spending money.

segments.chapter: Zutty's stroke and friends
segments.title: The Singletons and Nesuhi Ertegun: a foursome in California
segments.summary: In California the Singletons and the Erteguns dined together, held holiday dinners and played poker; Ertegun tells people Zutty is his oldest friend.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Marge mistakes Johnny Hodges for Zutty at the Ritz Hotel
segments.summary: In a Chicago hotel with the Ellington band, a tipsy Marge went to the wrong floor and pulled the sheet off Johnny Hodges, accusing his wife Cue of being with Zutty; they have called her wife-in-law since.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Opening the Three Deuces with his own band and asking for a raise
segments.summary: Zutty's band at the Three Deuces had Vernon York, Horace Eubanks, Leonard Bibb and Henry Gordon and lasted a year; Marge made him ask Sam Beer for a raise.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Hiring Art Tatum and Simp Green for the Three Deuces
segments.summary: On Sam Beer's vacation trip Zutty hired Simp Green, a singer-dancer, and went to Cleveland to bring in Art Tatum, who earned a hundred dollars a week for the first time.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Roy Eldridge's band at the Three Deuces, with Zutty featured
segments.summary: After Fletcher Henderson's Grand Terrace troubles and the flooding of the Three Deuces floor, Roy Eldridge's band came in with Joe Eldridge, Truck Parham, Teddy Cole and Johnny Collins while Zutty remained the feature.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: The Roy Eldridge records and the band breaking up
segments.summary: The group recorded a Heckler's Hop session and sides for Mildred Bailey; Roy took sick from fatigue, the band broke up, and Tatum took over.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Driving to New York with fifty cents and Wellman Braud's help
segments.summary: They drove east in a new Ford, ate salted peanuts and arrived in Harlem with fifty cents; Wellman Braud fed them and found a room at Miss Cotton's, the House of Meditation.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Mezz Mezzrow and Joe Marsala's Sunday jam session at the Hickory House
segments.summary: Mezz took them to the Hickory House where Joe Marsala gave Zutty his first New York job, a thirty-five-dollar Sunday jam session that paid his first car installment.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Mezzrow's band and Nick's, with Bobby Hackett
segments.summary: Dance reads the biography of Mezzrow's Disciples of Swing and Nick's; Zutty was an added attraction at Nick's with Bobby Hackett, and Bechet came later.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: The Vanguard, Nick's and the first band at Jimmy Ryan's
segments.summary: After Nick fired Zutty he went to the Village Vanguard, then Ryan's from 1941 to 1943, leading the first band with Sidney DeParis, Joe Eldridge, Don Frye and Al Hall, later LeRoy Tibbs.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Stormy Weather and the move to Billy Berg's in Los Angeles
segments.summary: After making Stormy Weather in California, Zutty was booked into Billy Berg's with a quartet of Joe Eldridge, Kenny Watts and Bass Hill, and Marge reluctantly agreed to go.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Joe Eldridge, Roy's brother, and the lack of help
segments.summary: Zutty did everything for Joe Eldridge, and thought Roy did not help his brother; Benny Carter gave Joe copying work in California.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Marge dislikes California; dogs and the house
segments.summary: Marge says California's sunshine failed for three months, she and the dog Barney hated living with Jimmy Mundy's Chow dogs, then bought a house nearby and became attached to Dooley Wilson's family.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Long residencies at the Vanguard and Ryan's
segments.summary: Berg's picked up Zutty's option for a year; Dance and Marge praise long residencies, and Zutty tells how he opened Ryan's and changed the Vanguard's clientele, bringing the band to Ryan's after Milt Gabler's sessions.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Bubber Miley: sweet man, his growl, and leaving Duke
segments.summary: Zutty says Bubber Miley was the sweetest man, who came to dinner; they recall his growl on the first Ellington broadcast and wonder if drink, or two trumpeters, ended his time with Duke.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Ralph Cooper's band at the M and S Theater
segments.summary: Marge recalls the M and S Theater band in new blue uniforms, led by the dancer Ralph Cooper who could not hold a saxophone, with Henry Goodwin and Gus McLeod on trumpets; it rivalled the Apollo and was soon renamed the Harlem.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: After Billy Berg's: Paul Howard and a year with T-Bone Walker
segments.summary: After Berg's Zutty played the Streets of Paris and Swanee Inn, a night or two with Paul Howard, then a year in T-Bone Walker's band, with Mingus on bass, playing Ellington tunes at the Brown Sisters' club past Watts.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: The Navy drummer Dave stays with them and Rudy Vallee takes him off
segments.summary: A drummer called Dave, just out of the Navy, stayed two weeks in the Singletons' California house, got drunk, and then went off to live with Rudy Vallee, leaving Marge a jacket and Zutty his practice pad.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Billy Berg's new place, the Orson Welles show and Teddy Bunn
segments.summary: Dance reads the biography for spring 1945, when Zutty played Berg's new club on Vine Street; they talk about Teddy Bunn, last heard with Louis Jordan's band.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Six-week college tour with Nappy Lamare's band
segments.summary: Zutty went on the road with Nappy Lamare, Brad Gowans, Stew Fletcher and Pud Brown, playing West Coast colleges for about six weeks.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Recording and movie work in California
segments.summary: Marge says Zutty earned good money in California from many record dates, including for Capitol, and small movie parts.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: The Slim Gaillard trio and Hollywood nights
segments.summary: Zutty played in Slim Gaillard's trio with Tiny Brown at a packed Hollywood club of movie stars, where Slim acted out pictures on the stand, and then toured East in theaters.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Taking Slim Gaillard's money seriously: William Morris and the box office
segments.summary: Zutty insisted on being paid by theater management through the William Morris office because Slim Gaillard was known to take money; Slim lost his house at auction for unpaid taxes.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Wingy Manone, Eddie Condon and the Chicago Blue Note
segments.summary: Dance reads a string of 1946-49 jobs; Zutty was with Wingy Manone in California but joined Condon in Chicago, with Bobby Hackett, Bud Freeman and Peanuts Hucko at the Blue Note.

segments.chapter: Chicago, New York and California, 1935-49
segments.title: Back in California: Club 47 and the Knotty Pine
segments.summary: California was their headquarters: Zutty returned to Club 47 after the road tour, then played the cowboy joint Knotty Pine with Bernie Billings and Bobby Troup.

segments.chapter: Europe, films and later years
segments.title: Sailing to Europe in 1951 with Mezz and Hot Lips Page
segments.summary: Dance reads Art Hodes, Bobby Hackett and Bernie Billings dates; Zutty sailed to Europe in November 1951 and played in Belgium with Mezz Mezzrow and Hot Lips Page.

segments.chapter: Europe, films and later years
segments.title: The Belgian casino with its New Orleans Room
segments.summary: The three-month season was at a big Belgian gambling casino with seven rooms, a concert room, a movie theater and a New Orleans Room, where musicians could not gamble.

segments.chapter: Europe, films and later years
segments.title: The Bill Coleman tour, tired of Europe, and the Paris hotel
segments.summary: Zutty was ready to go home, but Marge urged him to stay and tour with Bill Coleman and Dickie Wells; Marge praises their hotels, with hot water around the clock in Paris.

segments.chapter: Europe, films and later years
segments.title: Learning French in Europe
segments.summary: Zutty's New Orleans background helped him speak French well, while Marge learned to count from a Balenciaga acquaintance and sometimes needed an English speaker in shops.

segments.chapter: Europe, films and later years
segments.title: Back in New York at Ryan's with Wilbur DeParis
segments.summary: Dance runs down the post-Europe jobs at Stuyvesant Casino, Central Plaza, the Metropole and Ryan's, where Zutty joined Wilbur DeParis, then Tony Parenti and Max Kaminsky.

segments.chapter: Europe, films and later years
segments.title: Zutty's film credits: Stormy Weather, New Orleans and others
segments.summary: Dance and the Singletons recall his movies, including Stormy Weather, New Orleans, Turned Up Toes, a film with Cesar Romero and Paul Douglas, and A Song Is Born with Danny Kaye.

segments.chapter: Europe, films and later years
segments.title: Giving up the California house before Europe
segments.summary: Everyone expected Zutty could return to Club 47, but they left California for Europe and the owner's estate later asked them to buy the house they had been renting.
